The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-6$.

title: Which Model Fits the Measurements?
context: A meter reading was recorded once per minute for five minutes; $x$ counts the minutes and $y$ is the reading. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The table is consistent with a linear model.
A linear rule through the table has slope $-3$.
The average rate of change between $x=0$ and $x=4$ is $-3$.
The table is produced by the rule $y=-3x+10$.
The second differences of the $y$-values are constant and equal to $-3$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

List the five readings and subtract neighbours; constant first differences are the fingerprint of a line.

$$y:\ 10,\ 7,\ 4,\ 1,\ -2$$

$$\text{first differences}:\ -3,\ -3,\ -3,\ -3$$

The steps are all equal, so a linear model fits the table exactly.

The table is consistent with a linear model.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The slope of a line through equally spaced rows is one first-difference divided by the spacing of the inputs.

$$\text{first differences}:\ -3,\ -3,\ -3,\ -3$$

$$m=\frac{-3}{1}$$

$$m=-3$$

Every pair of consecutive minutes produces the same drop of $3$.

A linear rule through the table has slope $-3$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

An average rate over a stretch uses only the two end rows: the change of the reading divided by the change of time.

$$y(0)=10$$

$$y(4)=-2$$

$$x=\frac{-2-10}{4-0}$$

$$x=\frac{-12}{4}$$

$$x=-3$$

On a line that average equals the slope, already found to be $-3$.

The average rate between $x=0$ and $x=4$ is $-3$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Substitute the claimed rule into the listed minutes; matching the intercept and the slope already pins a line down, and the remaining rows are a check.

$$y=-3x+10$$

$$y=0\mapsto 10,\quad 1\mapsto 7,\quad 2\mapsto 4,\quad 3\mapsto 1,\quad 4\mapsto -2$$

Every row of the table is reproduced.

The table is produced by $y=-3x+10$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Second differences of a line are zero, because the first differences are already constant.

$$\text{first differences}:\ -3,\ -3,\ -3,\ -3$$

$$\text{second differences}:\ 0,\ 0,\ 0$$

They are constant, but the constant is $0$, not the claimed $-3$ (which was the first difference, not the second).

The second differences equal $0$, not $-3$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The table is the whole stem, so read it as a list of pairs.

$$\left(0,10\right),\ \left(1,7\right),\ \left(2,4\right),\ \left(3,1\right),\ \left(4,-2\right)$$

The inputs are equally spaced, which makes the differences of neighbouring outputs the fastest diagnostic tool available.

$$\text{first}:\ -3,\ -3,\ -3,\ -3\qquad \text{second}:\ 0,\ 0,\ 0$$

Constant first differences mean a line, and the slope is one difference divided by the spacing of the inputs.

$$y=-3x+10$$

title: A Negative Stretch Keeps the Zeros
context: A scaled factored parabola is written $p(x)=-3\left(x+2\right)\left(x-5\right)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The roots of $p$ are $-2$ and $5$.
The graph of $p$ opens downwards.
The axis of symmetry of $p$ is the line $x=\frac{3}{2}$.
The leading coefficient of $p$ is $3$.
The two roots of $p$ multiply to $-10$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A product vanishes exactly when one of its factors does, and the stretch $-3$ never vanishes, so the brackets already display the roots.

$$p(x)=-3(x+2)(x-5)$$

$$p(x)=0$$

$$x=-2$$

$$x=5$$

No expanding is required, and there are no other zeros.

The roots are $-2$ and $5$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The stretch in front of the two brackets is the leading coefficient once they are multiplied out, including its minus sign.

$$p(x)=-3(x+2)(x-5)$$

$$a=-3$$

$$-3<0$$

A negative stretch sends both arms downwards, so the turning point is the highest point of the graph.

The graph opens downwards.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The axis sits halfway between the two roots, which the brackets already name; the stretch $-3$ does not move that midpoint.

$$x=\frac{-2+5}{2}$$

$$x=\frac{3}{2}$$

Expanding and using $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$ recovers the same line: $p(x)=-3x^{2}+9x+30$ gives

$$x=-\frac{9}{2\cdot(-3)}$$

The axis is $x=\frac{3}{2}$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The leading coefficient is the stretch in front of the two brackets, including its minus sign.

$$p(x)=-3(x+2)(x-5)$$

$$p(x)=-3x^{2}+9x+30$$

$$a=-3$$

The claim reports $3$, which drops that minus sign.

The leading coefficient is $-3$, not $3$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Multiply the two roots sitting in the brackets; the stretch in front does not change the product of the zeros.

$$(-2)\cdot 5=-10$$

The same product is the constant term divided by the leading coefficient after expanding.

$$P=\frac{30}{-3}$$

$$P=-10$$

The two roots multiply to $-10$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Only one parabola is in play here.

$$p(x)=-3\left(x+2\right)\left(x-5\right)$$

Multiplying out puts the same rule in standard form, where every coefficient can be read off directly.

$$p(x)=-3x^{2}+9x+30$$

Completing the square locates the turning point, and Vieta's relations give the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots without solving anything.

$$
\text{vertex} = \left(\frac{3}{2},\frac{147}{4}\right),\qquad S = 3,\qquad P = -10
$$

Because the discriminant is positive the parabola meets the $x$-axis in two points, and factoring recovers them.

$$
\Delta = 441,\qquad x_{1} = -2,\qquad x_{2} = 5
$$

The arms open downwards, so the turning point is the highest point of the graph and the largest value is $\frac{147}{4}$.

title: A Parabola With the $y$-Axis as Its Mirror
context: The parabola $p$ has the rule $p(x)=2x^{2}-18$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graph of $p$ is symmetric about the $y$-axis.
The values $p(-3)$ and $p(3)$ are equal.
The roots of $p$ are $3$ and $-3$.
The two roots of $p$ multiply to $9$.
The smallest value taken by $p$ is $-18$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Symmetry about the $y$-axis means the formula is unchanged when $x$ is replaced by $-x$.

$$p(x)=2x^{2}-18$$

$$p(-x)=2(-x)^{2}-18$$

$$p(-x)=2x^{2}-18$$

$$p(-x)=p(x)$$

Equivalently the middle coefficient is $0$, so the axis formula returns $x=0$, the vertical coordinate axis itself.

The graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Opposite inputs sit at equal distance from the axis $x=0$, so they must return the same height; compute both to see it.

$$p(-3)=2\cdot 9-18$$

$$p(-3)=0$$

$$p(3)=2\cdot 9-18$$

$$p(3)=0$$

Both values equal $0$. That is no accident: $p$ is an even function.

The two values agree.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Set the given formula equal to zero and divide by the leading coefficient $2$.

$$2x^{2}-18 = 0$$

$$x^{2} = 9$$

$$x=-3$$

$$x=3$$

Both values really make $p$ vanish, and they sit symmetrically about the axis $x=0$.

The roots are $-3$ and $3$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Multiply the two roots just found, or read the product from the coefficients $P=c/a$.

$$(-3)\cdot 3=-9$$

$$P=\frac{-18}{2}$$

$$P=-9$$

The claim reports $9$, which drops the minus sign coming from the negative constant term.

The product is $-9$, not $9$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

With no $x$ term the turning point sits on the vertical axis, so evaluate the given formula there.

$$p(0)=-18$$

The leading coefficient $2$ is positive, so the arms rise on both sides and the values never sink below that height.

$$p(x)=2x^{2}-18$$

$$2x^{2}-18\ge-18$$

The smallest value is $-18$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
A single quadratic rule carries every claim.

$$p(x)=2x^{2}-18$$

Two standard readings cover most of what follows: the vertex from the completed square, and the sum and product of the roots from the coefficients.

$$
\text{vertex} = \left(0,-18\right),\qquad S = 0,\qquad P = -9
$$

A positive discriminant puts two crossings on the $x$-axis, placed symmetrically around the axis of the parabola.

$$
\Delta = 144,\qquad x_{1} = -3,\qquad x_{2} = 3
$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-18$.

title: Rebuilding a Parabola From Its Zeros
context: A parabola $p$ has zeros $-4$ and $2$ and leading coefficient $3$; recover its rule before judging the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rule is $p(x)=3x^{2}+6x-24$.
The axis of symmetry of $p$ is the line $x=-1$.
The graph of $p$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=-24$.
The smallest value taken by $p$ is $-27$.
The two roots of $p$ add up to $4$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Two zeros and a leading coefficient rebuild a parabola: the zeros fix the factors and the coefficient fixes the stretch.

$$p(x)=3(x+4)(x-2)$$

Multiplying the brackets out puts the rule in standard form.

$$p(x)=3(x^{2}+2x-8)$$

$$p(x)=3x^{2}+6x-24$$

The rebuilt rule is the one printed in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The axis sits halfway between the two given zeros; the stretch $3$ does not move that midpoint.

$$x=\frac{-4+2}{2}$$

$$x=\frac{-2}{2}$$

$$x=-1$$

The coefficient formula on the rebuilt rule $3x^{2}+6x-24$ returns the same line.

$$x=-\frac{6}{2\cdot 3}$$

$$x=-\frac{6}{6}$$

$$x=-1$$

The axis is $x=-1$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The vertical intercept is the value at $x=0$ of the rebuilt product, which is the product of the two constant pieces times the stretch.

$$p(0)=3(0+4)(0-2)$$

$$p(0)=3\cdot 4\cdot(-2)$$

$$p(0)=-24$$

That is also the constant term of $3x^{2}+6x-24$.

The graph meets the $y$-axis at $y=-24$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The smallest value is the height on the axis $x=-1$, because the stretch $3$ is positive.

$$p(-1)=3(-1+4)(-1-2)$$

$$p(-1)=3\cdot 3\cdot(-3)$$

$$p(-1)=-27$$

The arms rise on both sides, so $-27$ is the smallest value and there is no largest one.

The smallest value is $-27$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The zeros were given as $-4$ and $2$, so their sum is ordinary arithmetic; the stretch $3$ never enters it.

$$-4+2=-2$$

The same sum is minus the middle coefficient of the rebuilt rule $p(x)=3x^{2}+6x-24$.

$$S=-\frac{6}{3}$$

$$S=-2$$

The claim reports $4$, which drops the minus sign (or confuses the sum with the gap $2-(-4)=6$).

The two roots add up to $-2$, not $4$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Two zeros and a leading coefficient describe a parabola completely: the zeros fix the factors and the coefficient fixes the vertical stretch.

$$p(x)=3\left(x+4\right)\left(x-2\right)$$

Multiplying the two brackets out puts the rule in standard form.

$$p(x)=3x^{2}+6x-24$$

The axis formula fixes the turning point, while the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots come out of the coefficients with no equation to solve.

$$
\text{vertex} = \left(-1,-27\right),\qquad S = -2,\qquad P = -8
$$

The discriminant comes out positive, so the graph cuts the $x$-axis twice, once on either side of the axis of symmetry.

$$
\Delta = 324,\qquad x_{1} = -4,\qquad x_{2} = 2
$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-27$.

title: A Line Fixed by a Slope and One Point
context: A line $u$ has slope $-\frac{1}{2}$ and passes through the point $(4,1)$; recover its rule before judging the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rule is $u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x+3$.
The graph of $u$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=3$.
The graph of $u$ crosses the $x$-axis at $x=6$.
$u$ is increasing.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A slope and one point determine a line: start at $(4,1)$ and walk along the slope $-\frac{1}{2}$.

$$u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}(x-4)+1$$

Expanding the bracket puts the rule in the shape $mx+q$.

$$u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x+2+1$$

$$u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x+3$$

The rebuilt rule is the one printed in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The height at $x=0$ is the intercept of the rebuilt line. Starting at height $3$ and walking four units with slope $-\frac{1}{2}$ lands at $3-2=1$, recovering the given point $(4,1)$.

$$u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x+3$$

$$u(0)=3$$

The graph meets the $y$-axis at $y=3$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The rebuilt line is $u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x+3$. The graph crosses the horizontal axis where that height is zero, so isolate $x$.

$$-\frac{1}{2}x+3=0$$

$$x=6$$

Substituting back gives

$$u(6)=-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6+3$$

$$u(6)=0$$

so it is a genuine zero and the only one, because a non-constant line crosses the axis once.

The crossing is at $x=6$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The rebuilt line is $u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x+3$, obtained from the slope $-\frac{1}{2}$ and the point $(4,1)$. Substitute $x=-2$ and simplify term by term.

$$u(-2)=-\frac{1}{2}\cdot(-2)+3$$

The product of two minus signs is positive, so the slope term contributes $+1$.

$$u(-2)=1+3$$

$$u(-2)=4$$

The value at $x=-2$ is $4$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The direction of a line is decided by the sign of its slope. The given slope is already negative.

$$u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x+3$$

$$m=-\frac{1}{2}$$

$$-\frac{1}{2}<0$$

Because the slope is negative, every step to the right lowers the height:

$$u(0)=3$$

$$u(2)=2$$

The function is decreasing, not increasing.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
A slope and one point are enough for a line: start at the given point and walk along the slope.

$$u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}\left(x-4\right)+1$$

Expanding the bracket puts the rule in the familiar shape.

$$u(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x+3$$

Two numbers describe it completely: the slope, which is the change of height per unit step, and the height above the origin.

$$
m = -\frac{1}{2},\qquad u(0) = 3
$$

Setting the height to zero locates the single crossing of the $x$-axis, and the sign of the slope fixes the direction once and for all.

$$
-\frac{1}{2}x+3 = 0\Rightarrow x = 6
$$

title: Who Wins Far to the Right?
context: A non-constant line $f$ and a parabola $g$ whose leading coefficient $a$ is nonzero are given; no numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $a$ is positive, then $g(x)>f(x)$ for all sufficiently large $x$.
If $a$ is positive, then $g(x)>f(x)$ for every real $x$.
If $a$ is negative, then $g(x)<f(x)$ for all sufficiently large $x$.
There is a line whose graph stays above the whole graph of an upward-opening parabola.
If $g$ opens upwards, then the difference $g-f$ is bounded below on $\mathbb{R}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write $f(x)=mx+q$ and $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ with $a>0$, and compare them through their difference.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q)$$

Subtracting a line never touches the coefficient of $x^{2}$, so the difference is again a parabola opening upwards.

$$g(x)-f(x)=a(x-h)^{2}+k\quad\text{with }a>0$$

Once $x$ lies to the right of the larger root the difference is strictly positive and grows without bound, because the square term outruns the rest.

The parabola therefore stays above the line for all sufficiently large $x$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Winning the race far to the right says nothing about a bounded stretch near the origin, so a single pair settles the claim.

$$g(x)=x^{2}$$

$$f(x)=x$$

Here $a=1>0$ and the line is non-constant. Halfway between the two meetings the line is the higher of the two.

$$g\bigl(\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)=\tfrac{1}{4}$$

$$f\bigl(\tfrac{1}{2}\bigr)=\tfrac{1}{2}$$

The difference $x^{2}-x=x(x-1)$ is negative on the whole interval between $0$ and $1$.

An upward-opening parabola can dip below a line on a bounded stretch.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The same comparison works upside down: subtracting the line leaves $a$ untouched, and now $a<0$.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q),\quad a<0$$

A downward-opening parabola is positive at most between its two roots, so beyond the larger of them the difference stays strictly negative and falls without bound.

$$x\text{ large}\implies g(x)-f(x)<0\implies g(x)<f(x)$$

Far enough to the right the line sits above the parabola.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A line staying above the whole graph would mean $g-f$ never becomes positive, so look at what that difference actually does when $a>0$.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q),\quad a>0$$

Being an upward-opening parabola, this difference grows beyond every bound as $x$ increases. With $g(x)=x^{2}$ and any line $f(x)=mx+q$ the difference is positive as soon as $x$ is large enough.

$$x^{2}-mx-q>0\text{ for all large }x$$

Every line is eventually overtaken, so no line can stay above an upward-opening parabola everywhere.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Bounded below means the values never sink past some fixed level, and for a parabola that level is the vertex height.

$$d(x)=g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q),\quad a>0$$

Completing the square isolates a non-negative square multiplied by the positive number $a$.

$$d(x)=a(x-h)^{2}+k\ge k\quad\text{for every real }x$$

The number $k$ is attained at the vertex of $d$, so it is a genuine smallest value.

The difference is bounded below on all of $\mathbb{R}$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
No numbers are on offer, so the meetings of the graphs have to be counted through the difference $g-f$ in general form.

$$g(x)-f(x)=0$$

Common points of a line and a parabola solve a single quadratic equation, so there can never be more than two of them. Far out on either side the $x^{2}$ term outgrows every linear term, so the parabola decides who ends up on top.

title: When Is the Difference Still Curved?
context: A line $f$ and a parabola $g$ with nonzero leading coefficient $a$ are given; write $d=g-f$ for their difference. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The coefficient of $x^{2}$ in $d$ is nonzero.
Some choice of $f$ makes $d$ a linear function.
Some choice of $f$ makes the coefficient of $x$ in $d$ vanish.
If the coefficient of $x$ in $d$ vanishes, then the axis of $g$ is the vertical coordinate axis.
Whatever $f$ is, the graph of $d$ opens in the same direction as the graph of $g$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write $f(x)=mx+q$ and $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ with $a\neq 0$, and expand the difference. Only the parabola can contribute a square term.

$$d(x)=(ax^{2}+bx+c)-(mx+q)$$

$$d(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q)$$

The line only ever touches the $x$ term and the constant term; the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is copied from $g$ and is nonzero because $g$ is a parabola.

That coefficient equals $a\neq 0$ whatever $f$ is.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Making $d$ a line would require the square term to disappear, so ask which choice of $f$ could cancel it.

$$d(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q)$$

A line has no $x^{2}$ term at all, so subtracting it leaves $a$ in place; the only way to reach a zero coefficient would be $a=0$, which is excluded.

$$a\neq 0$$

$$d\text{ still has a square term}$$

No choice of $f$ can flatten the difference into a line.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The coefficient of $x$ in the difference is the gap between the middle coefficient of $g$ and the slope of $f$, so it can be steered by choosing the slope.

$$d(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q)$$

Setting $m=b$ makes that gap vanish; the line $f(x)=bx$ is one such choice, and any other intercept works equally well.

$$m = b$$

$$d(x)$$

$$d(x)=ax^{2}+(c-q)$$

One suitable line removes the $x$ term completely.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A vanishing $x$ term in $d$ means $m=b$, and that condition concerns the difference, not the original parabola.

$$b-m = 0$$

$$d(x)=ax^{2}+(c-q)$$

Take a concrete pair where this happens while the axis of $g$ is off the vertical coordinate axis.

$$g(x)=x^{2}+2x$$

$$f(x)=2x$$

$$d(x)$$

$$f(x)=x^{2}$$

Here the $x$ term of $d$ has vanished, yet the axis of $g$ is $x=-1$.

The condition on $d$ says nothing about where the axis of $g$ sits.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The opening direction is the sign of the coefficient of $x^{2}$, so compare that single number for $g$ and for $d$.

$$d(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q)$$

Subtracting a line changes the $x$ term and the constant term only, so both graphs carry the same leading coefficient $a$.

$$a>0$$

$$\text{both open upwards}\qquad a<0$$

$$\text{both open downwards}$$

The two parabolas always turn the same way, whichever line is subtracted.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
No coefficients are fixed, so the letters $a$, $b$ and $c$ have to be handled through the formulas that hold for every parabola.

$$
x = -\frac{b}{2a},\qquad g(x)-f(x) = 0
$$

The axis of symmetry sits at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, so it follows the first two coefficients and ignores the constant term entirely. Common points of a line and a parabola solve a single quadratic equation, so there can never be more than two of them.

title: Touching at the Vertex
context: A horizontal line $f(x)=2$ sits next to the parabola $g(x)=x^{2}+2x+3$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graphs of $f$ and $g$ have exactly one point in common.
That common point is the vertex of the graph of $g$.
At the common point the two graphs have the same slope.
The two graphs cross each other at that point.
The function $g$ has two distinct real roots.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Common points solve $g(x)=f(x)$, so bring everything to one side and see what kind of expression appears.

$$x^{2}+2x+3-2=x^{2}+2x+1$$

$$x^{2}+2x+3-2=0$$

The left-hand side is a perfect square, which can vanish only where the bracket itself does.

$$(x+1)^{2} = 0$$

$$x$$

$$x^{2}+2x+3-2=-1$$

A double root counts as a single point of the plane, namely $(-1,2)$, and there is nowhere else the two graphs can agree.

Exactly one point is shared.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The vertex sits on the axis $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, and its height is the value of $g$ there.

$$x=-\frac{2}{2\cdot 1}$$

$$x=-\frac{2}{2}$$

$$x=-1$$

$$g(-1)=1-2+3$$

$$g(-1)=1-2$$

$$g(-1)=-1$$

$$g(-1)=-1+3$$

$$g(-1)=2$$

So the vertex is $(-1,2)$, which is exactly the single common point found from $g=f$. Checking the line: $f(-1)=2$.

The contact happens at the vertex.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The line is horizontal, so its slope is zero. At a vertex the chord slopes of the parabola collapse to zero as well: a step of size $h$ from $x=-1$ changes the height by a square.

$$g(-1+h)-g(-1)=((-1+h)^{2}+2(-1+h)+3)-2$$

$$g(-1+h)-g(-1)=h^{2}$$

Dividing by the step $h$ leaves $h$, which tends to $0$ as $h$ tends to $0$.

$$\frac{g(-1+h)-g(-1)}{h}=h\to 0$$

Both graphs therefore have slope $0$ at the contact point.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Crossing would mean the difference changes sign at the contact point, so track that sign.

$$g(x)-f(x)=(x+1)^{2}$$

A square is never negative, and here it is strictly positive on both sides of $x=-1$.

$$g(-2)-2=1$$

$$1>0$$

$$g(0)-2=1$$

$$1>0$$

The parabola stays above the line on either side and merely comes down to touch it once.

The graphs touch without crossing.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

Real roots of $g$ exist according to the sign of its discriminant.

$$\Delta=2^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 3$$

$$2^{2}=4$$

$$\Delta=4-4\cdot 1\cdot 3$$

$$\Delta=-8$$

$$\Delta=4-12$$

A negative discriminant leaves no real solution of $g(x)=0$. Completing the square says the same thing more directly.

$$g(x)=(x+1)^{2}+2$$

$$(x+1)^{2}+2\ge2>0$$

The lowest value is $2$, so the graph stays entirely above the horizontal axis.

There are no real roots, let alone two distinct ones.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Both rules are handed over with numbers already in place:

$$
f(x) = 2,\qquad g(x) = x^{2} + 2 x + 3
$$

No work beyond reading is needed for the slope, for the two values at $0$ and for the opening direction, which is upwards here because of the sign in front of $x^{2}$.

$$
m = 0,\qquad f(0) = 2,\qquad g(0) = 3,\qquad a = 1
$$

Since the parabola is concrete, the vertex can be computed once and reused: the axis first, then the height above it.

$$
g(x) = \left(x+1\right)^{2}+2,\qquad \text{vertex} = \left(-1,2\right)
$$

Vieta's relations read the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots of $g$ straight off the coefficients, and the discriminant of $g$ says how many real roots there are to sum in the first place.

$$
S = -2,\qquad P = 3,\qquad \Delta_{g} = -8
$$

Common points are the roots of $f-g$, and that difference is again a quadratic, so its discriminant settles the count: one here.

$$
f(x)-g(x) = - x^{2} - 2 x - 1,\qquad \Delta = 0
$$

title: The Quadratic Hidden Behind a Data Table
context: The five pairs below come from one polynomial rule of degree at most two. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The first differences of the $y$-values are constant.
The second differences of the $y$-values are constant and equal to $4$.
A quadratic rule through the table has leading coefficient $2$.
The table is produced by the rule $y=2x^{2}-3x+1$.
The $y$-values in the table are smallest at $x=1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

List the five outputs from the table and subtract neighbours; constant first differences would be the fingerprint of a line.

$$y:\ 1,\ 0,\ 3,\ 10,\ 21$$

$$\text{first differences}:\ -1,\ 3,\ 7,\ 11$$

The steps come in four different sizes, and they even change sign.

The first differences are not constant.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Differencing the first differences once more produces the second differences, which for a quadratic rule are constant.

$$\text{first differences}:\ -1,\ 3,\ 7,\ 11$$

$$\text{second differences}:\ 4,\ 4,\ 4$$

They are all equal to $4$, the value the claim names.

The second differences are constant and equal to $4$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

For inputs spaced by $1$, the constant second difference of a quadratic rule equals $2a$, so the leading coefficient can be read off the table.

$$\text{second difference}=2a$$

$$\text{second difference}=4$$

$$a=2$$

The leading coefficient of any quadratic through the table is therefore $2$.

A quadratic rule through the table has leading coefficient $2$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Substitute the claimed rule into the listed rows; for a quadratic, matching three rows already pins the rule down, and the remaining two are a check.

$$y=2x^{2}-3x+1$$

$$0\mapsto 1,\quad 1\mapsto 0,\quad 2\mapsto 3,\quad 3\mapsto 10,\quad 4\mapsto 21$$

Every pair is reproduced.

The table is produced by $y=2x^{2}-3x+1$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

A claim about the rows of the table is settled inside the table itself: compare the listed outputs and see where the smallest one sits.

$$y:\ 1,\ 0,\ 3,\ 10,\ 21$$

The smallest listed value is $0$, and it appears at $x=1$. The neighbouring values $1$ and $3$ are both larger.

The $y$-values in the table are smallest at $x=1$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The table is the whole stem, so read it as a list of pairs.

$$\left(0,1\right),\ \left(1,0\right),\ \left(2,3\right),\ \left(3,10\right),\ \left(4,21\right)$$

The inputs are equally spaced, which makes the differences of neighbouring outputs the fastest diagnostic tool available.

$$\text{first}:\ -1,\ 3,\ 7,\ 11\qquad \text{second}:\ 4,\ 4,\ 4$$

The first differences move while the second ones stand still, the signature of a parabola; the constant second difference is twice the leading coefficient times the squared spacing.

$$y=2x^{2}-3x+1$$

title: Turning Point, Zeros and a Horizontal Probe
context: Consider the quadratic $q(x)=x^{2}-10x+21$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The vertex of the graph of $q$ is the point $\left(5,-4\right)$.
The roots of $q$ are $3$ and $7$.
The distance between the two roots of $q$ is $4$.
The smallest value taken by $q$ is $21$.
The horizontal line $y=-4$ meets the graph of $q$ at two different points.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The turning point sits on the axis $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, so compute that abscissa from the given coefficients and then the height.

$$q(x)=x^{2}-10x+21$$

$$x=-\frac{-10}{2}$$

$$x=5$$

$$q(5)=25-50+21$$

$$q(5)=25-50$$

$$q(5)=-25$$

$$q(5)=-25+21$$

$$q(5)=-4$$

The vertex is therefore the point $(5,-4)$.

That is the point named in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Set the given formula equal to zero. The discriminant first says how many roots there are.

$$\Delta=(-10)^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 21$$

$$\Delta=100-84$$

$$\Delta=16$$

A positive discriminant gives two distinct roots, and the quadratic factors as $(x-3)(x-7)$.

$$x=3$$

$$x=7$$

The zeros are $3$ and $7$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The two roots sit symmetrically on either side of the axis $x=5$, so their gap is the absolute difference of the roots.

$$|7-3|=4$$

The same gap can be read from the discriminant without listing the roots:

$$\frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{|a|}=\frac{\sqrt{16}}{1}$$

$$\frac{\sqrt{16}}{1}$$

$$\frac{\sqrt{\Delta}}{|a|}=4$$

Both routes agree. The distance between the two roots is $4$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The smallest value of an upward-opening parabola is the vertex height, not the constant term $21$ sitting at the end of the formula.

$$q(5)=-4$$

The leading coefficient $1$ is positive, so the arms rise on both sides and the values never sink below $-4$.

$$q(x)\ge -4$$

The smallest value is $-4$, not the intercept $21$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The horizontal line $y=-4$ meets the parabola where $q(x)=-4$, that is where $q(x)+4=0$.

$$q(x)+4=x^{2}-10x+25$$

$$q(x)+4=(x-5)^{2}$$

A square vanishes at one abscissa only, namely the axis $x=5$. The level $y=-4$ is the vertex height itself, so the line touches the graph once instead of cutting it twice.

There is only one meeting.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Everything below refers to the same parabola.

$$q(x)=x^{2}-10x+21$$

Before testing anything, it pays to write down the vertex together with the sum and the product of the roots, all three being coefficient arithmetic.

$$
\text{vertex} = \left(5,-4\right),\qquad S = 10,\qquad P = 21
$$

Because the discriminant is positive the parabola meets the $x$-axis in two points, and factoring recovers them.

$$
\Delta = 16,\qquad x_{1} = 3,\qquad x_{2} = 7
$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-4$.

title: Fuel Use Against Cruising Speed
context: For a lorry cruising at $x$ kilometres per hour, the fuel used on a fixed route is modelled by $F(x)=\frac{1}{50}x^{2}-2x+80$ litres. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The fuel use is smallest at $x=50$.
The smallest possible fuel use equals $30$ litres.
Between $x=20$ and $x=40$ the fuel use changes at an average rate of $-1$ litres per unit of $x$.
The fuel use is never zero.
At $x=100$ the fuel use equals $80$ litres.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Fuel use follows a parabola, so the most economical speed is the abscissa of the turning point, read from the first two coefficients.

$$F(x)=\frac{1}{50}x^{2}-2x+80$$

$$a=\frac{1}{50},\ b$$

$$a=-2$$

$$x=-\frac{-2}{2\cdot\frac{1}{50}}$$

$$x=50$$

The leading coefficient $\frac{1}{50}$ is positive, so the model falls to that input and rises afterwards.

The fuel use is smallest at $x=50$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The extreme fuel use is the height of the turning point, so evaluate the model at $x=50$.

$$F(50)=\frac{1}{50}\cdot 50^{2}-2\cdot 50+80$$

$$50^{2}=2500$$

$$F(50)=\frac{1}{50}\cdot 2500-2\cdot 50+80$$

$$F(50)=50^{2}-100+80$$

$$50^{2}=2500$$

$$F(50)=50-100+80$$

$$F(50)=50-100$$

$$F(50)=-50$$

$$F(50)=-50+80$$

$$F(50)=30$$

Because $a=\frac{1}{50}>0$ this height is the smallest value the model ever reaches.

The smallest fuel use is $30$ litres.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

An average rate compares the change of fuel use with the change of speed, so evaluate both endpoints first and then divide.

$$F(20)=\frac{400}{50}-40+80$$

$$F(20)=48$$

$$F(40)=\frac{1600}{50}-80+80$$

$$F(40)=32$$

$$\frac{F(40)-F(20)}{40-20}=\frac{-16}{20}$$

$$\frac{F(40)-F(20)}{40-20}=-\frac{4}{5}$$

The average rate over that stretch is $-\frac{4}{5}$, not the claimed $-1$.

The claimed rate $-1$ is wrong.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Fuel use hits zero exactly when the quadratic has a real root, so compute the discriminant.

$$\Delta=(-2)^{2}-4\cdot\frac{1}{50}\cdot 80$$

$$\Delta=4-\frac{16}{5}$$

$$\Delta=-\frac{12}{5}$$

A negative discriminant keeps the whole graph on one side of the horizontal axis. The vertex height $30$ already sits strictly above zero.

$$F(50)=30$$

$$30>0$$

The model never returns a zero fuel use.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Substitute the cruising speed $100$ into the model and simplify term by term.

$$F(x)=\frac{1}{50}x^{2}-2x+80$$

$$F(100)=\frac{1}{50}\cdot 100^{2}-2\cdot 100+80$$

$$100^{2}=10000$$

$$F(100)=\frac{1}{50}\cdot 10000-2\cdot 100+80$$

$$F(100)=200-200+80$$

$$F(100)=200-200$$

$$F(100)=0$$

$$F(100)=0+80$$

$$F(100)=80$$

The square term and the linear term cancel, leaving the constant $80$.

The fuel use at $x=100$ is $80$ litres.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The story reduces to one formula and the quantities it links.

$$F(x)=\frac{1}{50}x^{2}-2x+80$$

The completed square hands over the turning point, and Vieta's relations hand over the sum and the product of the roots.

$$
\text{vertex} = \left(50,30\right),\qquad S = 100,\qquad P = 4000
$$

A negative discriminant keeps the graph entirely on one side of the $x$-axis.

$$\Delta=-\frac{12}{5}$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $30$.

title: A Parabola Pinned by Its Vertex and One Point
context: A parabola $q$ has its vertex at $(3,-8)$ and passes through the point $(1,0)$; recover its rule before judging the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rule is $q(x)=2x^{2}-12x+10$.
The roots of $q$ are $1$ and $5$.
The graph of $q$ meets the $y$-axis at $y=10$.
The leading coefficient of $q$ is $2$.
The horizontal line $y=-8$ meets the graph of $q$ at two different points.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A vertex already fixes the shape up to one stretch factor, so write the parabola in completed-square form and let the extra point decide the factor.

$$q(x)=a(x-3)^{2}-8$$

Substituting the point $(1,0)$ leaves one equation for $a$.

$$0 = a(1-3)^{2}-8$$

$$a$$

$$q(x)=2$$

Expanding the square puts the rule in standard form.

$$q(x)=2x^{2}-12x+10$$

The rebuilt rule is the one printed in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

One root is already handed over as the extra point $(1,0)$. The axis is $x=3$, so the other root is the mirror of $1$ in that axis.

$$3-(1-3)=5$$

Checking against the rebuilt formula $q(x)=2(x-3)^{2}-8$: expanding gives

$$2x^{2}-12x+10=2(x-1)(x-5)$$

$$x=1$$

$$x=5$$

The zeros are $1$ and $5$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The vertical intercept is the value at $x=0$ of the completed-square form with the stretch $a=2$ forced by the extra point.

$$q(x)=2(x-3)^{2}-8$$

$$q(0)=2\cdot 9-8$$

$$q(0)=10$$

That is also the constant term of $2x^{2}-12x+10$.

The graph meets the $y$-axis at $y=10$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The stretch $a$ was forced by the extra point $(1,0)$. Substitute into the vertex form.

$$q(x)=a(x-3)^{2}-8$$

$$0=a\cdot(1-3)^{2}-8$$

$$0=4a-8$$

$$a=2$$

Expand to confirm the leading coefficient:

$$q(x)=2(x-3)^{2}-8$$

$$q(x)=2x^{2}-12x+10$$

The number multiplying $x^{2}$ is $2$. The leading coefficient is $2$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The horizontal line $y=-8$ is the vertex height itself, so meetings solve $q(x)+8=0$.

$$q(x)=2(x-3)^{2}-8$$

$$q(x)+8=2(x-3)^{2}$$

A square times $2$ vanishes at one abscissa only:

$$x=3$$

The line touches the graph once at the vertex instead of cutting it twice. There is only one meeting.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
A vertex already fixes the shape up to one stretch factor, so write the parabola in completed-square form and let the extra point decide the factor.

$$q(x)=a\left(x-3\right)^{2}-8$$

Substituting the point $(1,0)$ leaves one equation for $a$.

$$
0 = a\left(1-3\right)^{2}-8\Rightarrow a = 2
$$

Expanding the square puts the rule in standard form.

$$q(x)=2x^{2}-12x+10$$

Completing the square locates the turning point, and Vieta's relations give the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots without solving anything.

$$
\text{vertex} = \left(3,-8\right),\qquad S = 6,\qquad P = 5
$$

The discriminant comes out positive, so the graph cuts the $x$-axis twice, once on either side of the axis of symmetry.

$$
\Delta = 64,\qquad x_{1} = 1,\qquad x_{2} = 5
$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-8$.

title: A Profit Curve With Two Break-Even Points
context: A workshop's monthly profit in hundreds of euros, when $x$ machines are produced, is modelled by $P(x)=-x^{2}+24x-80$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The profit is largest at $x=12$.
The largest possible profit equals $64$.
The profit is zero exactly at $x=4$ and $x=20$.
Between $x=0$ and $x=10$ the profit changes at an average rate of $14$ per unit of $x$.
At $x=2$ the profit equals $0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Profit follows a parabola, so the best output is the abscissa of the turning point, read from the first two coefficients.

$$P(x)=-x^{2}+24x-80$$

$$a=-1,\ b$$

$$a=24$$

$$x=-\frac{24}{2\cdot(-1)}$$

$$x=12$$

The leading coefficient $-1$ is negative, so the model rises up to that input and falls afterwards.

The profit is largest at $x=12$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The extreme profit is the height of the turning point of $P(x)=-x^{2}+24x-80$, so evaluate the model at the axis $x=12$.

$$P(12)=-12^{2}+24\cdot 12-80$$

$$12^{2}=144$$

$$P(12)=-144+24\cdot 12-80$$

$$P(12)=64$$

$$P(12)=-144+288-80$$

Because $a=-1<0$ this height is the largest value the model ever reaches; the arms fall on both sides.

The largest profit is $64$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Profit is zero at the roots of the quadratic, so multiply by $-1$ and factor the resulting monic polynomial.

$$-x^{2}+24x-80 = 0$$

$$x^{2}-24x+80 = 0$$

$$(x-4)(x-20)=0$$

$$x=4$$

$$x=20$$

Those are the two break-even levels named in the claim.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

An average rate compares the change of profit with the change of output, so evaluate both endpoints first and then divide.

$$P(0)=-80$$

$$P(10)=-100+240-80$$

$$P(10)=-100+240$$

$$P(10)=140$$

$$P(10)=140-80$$

$$P(10)=60$$

$$\frac{P(10)-P(0)}{10-0}=\frac{140}{10}$$

$$\frac{P(10)-P(0)}{10-0}=14$$

The average rate over that stretch is $14$.

The average rate is $14$ per unit of $x$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The claim that two machines already break even is a substitution into the profit model.

$$P(x)=-x^{2}+24x-80$$

$$P(2)=-4+48-80$$

$$P(2)=-4+48$$

$$P(2)=44$$

$$P(2)=44-80$$

$$P(2)=-36$$

The true zeros sit at $x=4$ and $x=20$, so $x=2$ is still on the loss side of the first break-even.

The profit is $-36$, not $0$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The situation is captured by a single rule.

$$P(x)=-x^{2}+24x-80$$

Two standard readings cover most of what follows: the vertex from the completed square, and the sum and product of the roots from the coefficients.

$$
\text{vertex} = \left(12,64\right),\qquad S = 24,\qquad P = 80
$$

Two real roots follow from the positive discriminant, and the axis of symmetry sits exactly halfway between them.

$$
\Delta = 256,\qquad x_{1} = 4,\qquad x_{2} = 20
$$

The arms open downwards, so the turning point is the highest point of the graph and the largest value is $64$.

title: Half-Scaled Factors and the Values a Parabola Reaches
context: Consider $w(x)=\frac{1}{2}\left(x+1\right)\left(x-7\right)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The roots of $w$ are $-1$ and $7$.
The axis of symmetry of $w$ is the line $x=3$.
Expanding gives $w(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2}-3x-\frac{7}{2}$.
The smallest value taken by $w$ is $-8$.
$w(x)\ge 0$ holds for every real $x$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A product vanishes exactly when one of its factors does, and the stretch $\frac{1}{2}$ never vanishes, so the brackets already display the roots.

$$w(x)=\frac{1}{2}(x+1)(x-7)$$

$$w(x)=0$$

$$x=-1$$

$$x=7$$

No expanding is required, and there are no other zeros.

The roots are $-1$ and $7$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The axis sits halfway between the two roots named by the brackets; the stretch $\frac{1}{2}$ does not move that midpoint.

$$x=\frac{-1+7}{2}$$

$$x=\frac{6}{2}$$

$$x=3$$

Expanding and using $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$ recovers the same line: $w(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2}-3x-\frac{7}{2}$ gives

$$x=-\frac{-3}{2\cdot\frac{1}{2}}$$

The axis is $x=3$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Multiply the two brackets out and then apply the stretch $\frac{1}{2}$; the function itself does not change.

$$(x+1)(x-7)=x^{2}-6x-7$$

$$w(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2}-3x-\frac{7}{2}$$

Every coefficient agrees with the displayed expansion.

The expanded rule is $\frac{1}{2}x^{2}-3x-\frac{7}{2}$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The smallest value is the height on the axis $x=3$, because the stretch $\frac{1}{2}$ is positive.

$$w(3)=\frac{1}{2}(3+1)(3-7)$$

$$w(3)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot(-4)$$

$$w(3)=-8$$

The arms rise on both sides, so $-8$ is the smallest value and there is no largest one.

The smallest value is $-8$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

An inequality that has to hold for every real $x$ is a statement about the vertex height. The stretch $\frac{1}{2}$ is positive, so the values never drop below the vertex, but they do drop below $0$ between the two roots.

$$w(3)=-8$$

$$w(x)\ge -8\qquad w(3)=-8$$

$$-8<0$$

The claimed bound $0$ is broken at the turning point.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
There is one graph to study, and it is a parabola.

$$w(x)=\frac{1}{2}\left(x+1\right)\left(x-7\right)$$

Multiplying out puts the same rule in standard form, where every coefficient can be read off directly.

$$w(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^{2}-3x-\frac{7}{2}$$

The axis formula fixes the turning point, while the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots come out of the coefficients with no equation to solve.

$$
\text{vertex} = \left(3,-8\right),\qquad S = 6,\qquad P = -7
$$

Because the discriminant is positive the parabola meets the $x$-axis in two points, and factoring recovers them.

$$
\Delta = 16,\qquad x_{1} = -1,\qquad x_{2} = 7
$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-8$.

title: Heights of a Stone Recorded Every Second
context: A stone is launched upwards and its height above the ground is measured once per second. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The first differences of the $y$-values are constant.
The second differences of the $y$-values are constant and equal to $-10$.
The table is produced by the rule $y=-5x^{2}+30x$.
The $y$-values in the table are largest at $x=3$.
Continuing the pattern, the value at $x=5$ is $25$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

List the five heights from the table and subtract neighbours; constant first differences would be the fingerprint of a line.

$$y:\ 0,\ 25,\ 40,\ 45,\ 40$$

$$\text{first differences}:\ 25,\ 15,\ 5,\ -5$$

The steps come in four different sizes, and they even change sign after the peak.

The first differences are not constant.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → True

Differencing the first differences once more produces the second differences, which for a quadratic rule are constant.

$$\text{first differences}:\ 25,\ 15,\ 5,\ -5$$

$$\text{second differences}:\ -10,\ -10,\ -10$$

They are all equal to $-10$, the value the claim names.

The second differences are constant and equal to $-10$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Substitute the claimed rule into the listed seconds; for a quadratic, matching three rows already pins the rule down, and the remaining two are a check.

$$y=-5x^{2}+30x$$

$$0\mapsto 0,\quad 1\mapsto 25,\quad 2\mapsto 40,\quad 3\mapsto 45,\quad 4\mapsto 40$$

Every row of the table is reproduced.

The table is produced by $y=-5x^{2}+30x$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Compare the five listed heights and see where the largest one sits; the claim is about the table itself, not about a continuous model.

$$y:\ 0,\ 25,\ 40,\ 45,\ 40$$

The largest listed value is $45$, and it appears at $x=3$. The neighbouring values $40$ and $40$ are both smaller.

The $y$-values in the table are largest at $x=3$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The next first-difference shrinks by the constant second difference $-10$, so add $-5+(-10)=-15$ to the last height $40$.

$$40+(-15)=25$$

The same height comes from the quadratic rule already identified.

$$y(5)=-5\cdot 25+150$$

$$y(5)=25$$

The value at $x=5$ is $25$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The table is the whole stem, so read it as a list of pairs.

$$\left(0,0\right),\ \left(1,25\right),\ \left(2,40\right),\ \left(3,45\right),\ \left(4,40\right)$$

The inputs are equally spaced, which makes the differences of neighbouring outputs the fastest diagnostic tool available.

$$\text{first}:\ 25,\ 15,\ 5,\ -5\qquad \text{second}:\ -10,\ -10,\ -10$$

The first differences move while the second ones stand still, the signature of a parabola; the constant second difference is twice the leading coefficient times the squared spacing.

$$y=-5x^{2}+30x$$

title: Undoing a Line Around a Parabola
context: A non-constant line $f$ with inverse $f^{-1}$ is given together with a parabola $g$. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The inverse $f^{-1}$ is again a non-constant linear function.
The nested function $g(f^{-1}(x))$ is a quadratic function.
The nested function $f^{-1}(g(x))$ is a quadratic function.
The nested function $g(f^{-1}(x))$ always has the same roots as $g$.
The nested function $f^{-1}(g(x))$ always has the same axis of symmetry as $g$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write $f(x)=mx+q$ with $m\neq 0$ and undo it by solving $y=mx+q$ for $x$.

$$y = mx+q$$

$$x = \frac{y-q}{m}$$

The division is legitimate precisely because the line is non-constant, and the result is again a first-degree formula.

$$f^{-1}(y)=\frac{1}{m}y-\frac{q}{m}$$

Its slope is $1/m$, which is a non-zero number, so the inverse is not a constant function.

Undoing a non-constant line gives another non-constant line.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Nesting the inverse line inside the parabola substitutes a first-degree expression for $x$, so expand the square and collect the terms.

$$g\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)=a\left(\frac{x-q}{m}\right)^{2}+b\left(\frac{x-q}{m}\right)+c$$

The square of a first-degree expression reaches $x^{2}$ and stops there, and the coefficient it produces is the leading one of the composite.

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{2}=\frac{a}{m^{2}}\neq 0$$

It is non-zero because $a\neq 0$ and $m\neq 0$, so nothing cancels the square term.

The composite is again a parabola.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

In this order the parabola is computed first and the inverse line is applied afterwards, which merely rescales and shifts the values.

$$f^{-1}\left(g(x)\right)=\frac{g(x)-q}{m}$$

$$f^{-1}\left(g(x)\right)=\frac{a}{m}x^{2}+\frac{b}{m}x+\frac{c-q}{m}$$

The leading coefficient $a/m$ is again non-zero, so the square term survives the rescaling.

The composite is a parabola in this order as well.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Here the inverse line acts on the argument, so a root of the composite is an abscissa whose image under $f^{-1}$ is a root of $g$; the roots get moved rather than kept.

$$g\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)=0$$

$$f^{-1}(x)\text{ is a root of }g$$

Take the simplest concrete pair and follow the bookkeeping.

$$g(x)=x^{2}$$

$$f(x)=x+1$$

$$S=f^{-1}(x)$$

$$S=x-1$$

$$g\left(f^{-1}(x)\right)=\left(x-1\right)^{2}$$

The composite vanishes at $x=1$ while $g$ vanishes at $x=0$, so the two root sets are different.

Substituting inside the parabola shifts its roots.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

In this order the line acts after the parabola, and an operation performed on the values can only stretch or slide the graph vertically.

$$f^{-1}\left(g(x)\right)=\frac{a}{m}x^{2}+\frac{b}{m}x+\frac{c-q}{m}$$

Both the leading and the middle coefficient are divided by the same non-zero number $m$, so the quotient that produces the axis is unchanged.

$$-\frac{b/m}{2\left(a/m\right)}=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

The composite has exactly the same axis of symmetry as $g$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Everything is stated for a general parabola, so the reasoning runs on the structure of $ax^{2}+bx+c$ instead of on numbers.

$$
x = -\frac{b}{2a},\qquad f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x-q}{m}
$$

The axis of symmetry sits at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, so it follows the first two coefficients and ignores the constant term entirely. Nesting two polynomials multiplies their highest powers instead of adding them, so a line inside a parabola still leaves a parabola. Undoing a line gives another line, so wrapping it around a parabola cannot change the highest power that appears.

title: Mirroring a Line and a Parabola
context: A line $f$ and a parabola $g$ are mirrored by replacing $x$ with $-x$: write $\tilde f(x)=f(-x)$ and $\tilde g(x)=g(-x)$. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graphs of $\tilde f$ and $\tilde g$ meet exactly as often as those of $f$ and $g$.
If the graphs of $f$ and $g$ are tangent, then so are those of $\tilde f$ and $\tilde g$.
Mirroring in this way can turn two meetings into three.
The parabola $\tilde g$ always opens in the same direction as $g$.
The parabola $\tilde g$ always has the same axis of symmetry as $g$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Mirroring replaces $x$ by $-x$ in both formulas at once, so the equation for the common abscissas is transported by the same substitution.

$$\tilde f(x) = \tilde g(x)$$

$$f(-x) = g(-x)$$

Hence $x$ is a meeting abscissa of the mirrored pair exactly when $-x$ is a meeting abscissa of the original pair.

$$x\text{ solves the new equation}\iff -x\text{ solves the old one}$$

The assignment $x\mapsto -x$ pairs the two sets of solutions one against one, and a reflection can neither create nor destroy a meeting.

The counts agree.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Tangency is the algebraic statement that the difference has a repeated root, so mirror the difference and inspect its shape.

$$\tilde g(x)-\tilde f(x)=(g-f)(-x)$$

If the original graphs are tangent at abscissa $h$, the difference is a perfect square times its leading coefficient.

$$g(x)-f(x) = a(x-h)^{2}$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=(g-f)(-x)$$

$$\tilde g(x)-\tilde f(x)=a(x+h)^{2}$$

The mirrored difference is again a square with the same leading coefficient, now with its repeated root at $-h$.

The reflected graphs touch at the mirrored abscissa.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Write $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ and $f(x)=mx+q$. The number of meetings is governed by the difference, and mirroring keeps that difference quadratic with the same leading coefficient.

$$(g-f)(-x)=ax^{2}-(b-m)x+(c-q)$$

A quadratic equation has at most two real solutions, so three meetings are out of reach; the correspondence $x\mapsto -x$ shows the count was preserved exactly anyway.

$$a\neq 0$$

$$\text{at most two solutions}$$

Two meetings stay two meetings under a reflection.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The opening direction depends only on the coefficient of $x^{2}$, so mirror the formula $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ and read that coefficient off.

$$\tilde g(x)=a(-x)^{2}+b(-x)+c$$

$$\tilde g(x)=ax^{2}-bx+c$$

Squaring kills the minus sign, so the leading coefficient is still $a$ and its sign has not moved.

The mirrored parabola opens the same way as the original.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Reflecting across the vertical coordinate axis carries the axis of symmetry along with the graph, so compute where it lands.

$$\tilde g(x) = ax^{2}-bx+c$$

$$\text{axis }x=\frac{b}{2a}$$

The original axis is $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, so the two lines are opposites of each other and coincide only when $b=0$. A concrete pair makes the jump visible.

$$g(x) = (x-1)^{2}$$

$$\tilde g(x)=(x+1)^{2}$$

In this example the axis jumps from $x=1$ to $x=-1$, two different vertical lines.

The axis is mirrored too, so it generally moves.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
No coefficients are fixed, so the letters $a$, $b$ and $c$ have to be handled through the formulas that hold for every parabola.

$$
x = -\frac{b}{2a},\qquad \Delta = b^{2}-4ac
$$

The axis of symmetry sits at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, so it follows the first two coefficients and ignores the constant term entirely. The discriminant counts the real roots: two while it is positive, one when it vanishes and none once it turns negative. Replacing $x$ by $-x$ reflects a graph in the $y$-axis, and a parabola survives that swap exactly when its middle coefficient vanishes.

Both graphs are reflected at once, so the question is always which feature survives a reflection.

title: How Many Points Pin Down a Curve?
context: Three pairwise distinct points $P$, $Q$ and $R$ of the plane are given, no two of which lie on the same vertical line. No coordinates are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Exactly one linear function has both $P$ and $Q$ on its graph.
There is always at least one quadratic function having $P$, $Q$ and $R$ on its graph.
If $P$, $Q$ and $R$ are not collinear, then exactly one quadratic function has all three on its graph.
Infinitely many quadratic functions have both $P$ and $Q$ on their graphs.
A quadratic function and a linear function can agree at all three points.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Two points with different abscissas determine a slope, and the slope together with one of the points determines the whole line.

The denominator is non-zero because $P$ and $Q$ do not lie on a common vertical line, so this quotient is a genuine number; the intercept then has no freedom left.

Any line through both points must have this slope and this intercept, so no second one is possible.

Exactly one linear function passes through the two points.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Three points with distinct abscissas are always matched by exactly one formula of the shape $Ax^{2}+Bx+C$, but nothing guarantees that $A$ comes out non-zero.

$$A x_{P}^{2}+B x_{P}+C=y_{P},\quad\text{and likewise for }Q\text{ and }R$$

If the three points happen to be collinear, that unique solution is the line through them, with a vanishing square coefficient.

$$(0,0),\;(1,1),\;(2,2)$$

$$A=0,\quad B=1,\quad C=0$$

A quadratic function needs a non-zero coefficient of $x^{2}$, so in this configuration there is no quadratic function at all through the three points.

Collinear triples admit only a line, so the existence claim fails in general.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The three interpolation conditions form a system in the unknown coefficients, and distinct abscissas make it solvable in exactly one way.

$$
A x_{P}^{2}+B x_{P}+C=y_{P},\qquad A x_{Q}^{2}+B x_{Q}+C = y_{Q},\qquad A x_{R}^{2}+B x_{R}+C = y_{R}
$$

Subtracting the equations in pairs eliminates $C$ and then $B$, leaving one value for $A$, after which $B$ and $C$ follow in turn; every step divides only by differences of the abscissas, which are non-zero.

$$A=0$$

$$P,\,Q,\,R\text{ are collinear}$$

Since the points are assumed not to be collinear, the value obtained for $A$ is non-zero and the interpolating formula really is a quadratic one.

There is one such quadratic function and no more.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Passing through two points leaves one degree of freedom, and it can be displayed explicitly: start from the line through $P$ and $Q$ and add a term that vanishes at both abscissas.

$$g_{\lambda}(x)=\lambda(x-x_{P})(x-x_{Q})+mx+q$$

At $x=x_{P}$ and $x=x_{Q}$ the first summand is zero, so every member of this family contains both points, while the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is $\lambda$.

$$\lambda\neq 0$$

$$g_{\lambda}\text{ is a quadratic function}$$

Different non-zero values of $\lambda$ give different functions, and there are infinitely many of them.

Infinitely many parabolas pass through the same two points.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Agreement at a point means the difference of the two functions vanishes there, so study that difference.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q)\qquad a\neq 0$$

This is a quadratic expression, so it can vanish at two abscissas at most; three distinct abscissas are one too many.

$$x_{P},\,x_{Q},\,x_{R}\text{ distinct}$$

$$\text{three roots needed}$$

The abscissas are pairwise different because no two of the points share a vertical line, so the required third root cannot exist.

A parabola and a line can agree at two points but never at three.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The points stay unnamed, so the question is one of counting conditions against unknown coefficients.

$$
f(x) = mx+q,\qquad g(x) = ax^{2}+bx+c,\quad a\neq 0
$$

Two points with different abscissas settle exactly one line, and three non-collinear ones settle exactly one parabola.

The points stay anonymous, so only counting arguments can decide the claims.

title: Where the Difference Reaches Its Extreme
context: A line $f$ with slope $m$ and a parabola $g$ with nonzero leading coefficient $a$ are given; write $d=g-f$ for their difference. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Unless $m$ vanishes, the axis of $d$ differs from the axis of $g$.
The axis of $d$ never depends on $m$.
The coefficient of $x^{2}$ in $d$ equals $a$.
The function $d$ has a smallest value exactly when $a$ is positive.
If the graphs of $f$ and $g$ are tangent, then the vertex of $d$ lies on the horizontal coordinate axis.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write $f(x)=mx+q$ and $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$. Subtracting the line leaves the square term alone but shifts the middle coefficient by the slope, and the axis is built from exactly those two numbers.

$$d(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q)$$

$$
\text{axis of }d:\ x=-\frac{b-m}{2a},\qquad \text{axis of }g:\ x = -\frac{b}{2a}
$$

Subtracting one from the other leaves a single term, whose vanishing is controlled by the slope alone.

$$-\frac{b-m}{2a}-\Bigl(-\frac{b}{2a}\Bigr)=\frac{m}{2a}$$

As long as $m\neq 0$ this gap is non-zero, so the two axes are different vertical lines.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The axis of the difference was just computed, and the slope of the line sits right inside the formula.

$$\text{axis of }d:\ x=-\frac{b}{2a}+\frac{m}{2a}$$

Changing $m$ therefore slides that vertical line, and a concrete pair makes the movement visible.

$$g(x)=x^{2},\ m$$

$$g(x)= 0$$

$$\text{axis }x$$

$$m=2$$

$$\text{axis }x$$

$$m=1$$

Tilting the subtracted line moves the lowest point of the difference sideways.

The axis of $d$ does depend on the slope.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

A line contributes an $x$ term and a constant and nothing else, so the square term of the difference is inherited untouched.

$$d(x)=(ax^{2}+bx+c)-(mx+q)$$

$$d(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q)$$

Whatever slope and intercept the line has, the number in front of $x^{2}$ is still the leading coefficient of $g$, and it is non-zero.

That coefficient equals $a$ exactly.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Whether a parabola has a smallest value is decided by the direction in which it opens, and the difference opens the same way as $g$.

$$d(x)=a(x-h)^{2}+k$$

With $a>0$ the square is multiplied by a positive number, so the values never sink below the vertex height $k$, which is actually attained at $x=h$.

$$a>0$$

$$d(x)\ge k$$

$$a<0$$

$$d(x)\le k$$

With $a<0$ the picture is turned over: $k$ becomes the largest value and the arms fall without bound, so no smallest value exists.

A minimum exists precisely in the case $a>0$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Tangency of the two graphs means the equation $g(x)=f(x)$ has a repeated solution, that is, the difference has a double root.

$$d(x)=g(x)-f(x)$$

$$d(x)=a(x-h)^{2}$$

No constant is left over, so the vertex of $d$ sits at height zero.

$$d(h) = 0$$

$$\text{vertex}$$

$$d(x)=(h,0)$$

A point of height zero lies on the horizontal coordinate axis, and $h$ is the abscissa where the line touches the parabola.

The vertex of the difference lands exactly on that axis.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Since $a$, $b$ and $c$ are never given numbers, each claim has to survive for every admissible choice of them.

$$
x = -\frac{b}{2a},\qquad \Delta = b^{2}-4ac
$$

The axis of symmetry sits at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, so it follows the first two coefficients and ignores the constant term entirely. The discriminant counts the real roots: two while it is positive, one when it vanishes and none once it turns negative. Completed-square form puts the turning point at $(h,k)$, and the sign of $a$ decides whether $k$ is the smallest or the largest value taken.

title: Signs of the Roots from Sum and Product
context: A quadratic $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ with nonzero $a$ has two distinct real roots; write $S$ for their sum and $P$ for their product. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $P$ is negative, then the two roots have opposite signs.
If $P$ is positive and $S$ is negative, then both roots are negative.
If $P$ is negative and $a$ is positive, then $g$ takes a negative value at the origin.
If $P$ is positive, then both roots must be positive.
If $S$ vanishes, then the roots are opposites of each other and the axis is the vertical coordinate axis.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write $S=x_{1}+x_{2}$ and $P=x_{1}x_{2}$ for the two distinct real roots. The product alone already records their signs.

$$P=x_{1}x_{2}$$

$$P=\frac{c}{a}$$

A product of two real numbers is negative only when the factors have opposite signs, since equal signs give a positive product and a zero factor gives zero.

$$P<0$$

$$x_{1}x_{2}<0$$

$$\text{one root}<0<\text{the other}$$

Geometrically the parabola then crosses the horizontal axis once on each side of the origin.

A negative product forces roots of opposite signs.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The product fixes whether the signs agree, and the sum then decides which sign it is.

$$P>0$$

$$x_{1}\text{ and }x_{2}\text{ have the same sign}$$

Two positive numbers would add up to something positive, so a negative sum rules that case out and only the negative one survives.

$$S<0$$

$$x_{1}+x_{2}<0$$

$$\text{both roots}<0$$

For instance $g(x)=x^{2}+3x+2$ has $P=2>0$ and $S=-3<0$, with roots $-1$ and $-2$.

The two conditions together force both roots to be negative.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The value at the origin is the constant term, and the product of the roots expresses that term through $c=aP$.

$$P = \frac{c}{a}$$

$$c=aP$$

With $a>0$ and $P<0$ the product $aP$ is negative, so the constant term is negative.

$$g(0)=c$$

$$g(0)=aP<0$$

This matches the picture: an upward-opening parabola with one root on each side of the origin must dip below the horizontal axis in between, and the origin lies in that stretch.

The function takes a negative value at the origin.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A positive product only says the two roots share a sign; it does not say which sign, so one counterexample is enough.

$$g(x)=x^{2}+3x+2$$

$$g(x)=(x+1)(x+2)$$

$$x_{1}=-1$$

$$x_{2}=-2$$

$$P=2$$

$$2>0$$

The roots are distinct and real, the product is positive, yet both roots are negative. The missing extra hypothesis would have been a positive sum.

Positivity of the product leaves the negative case wide open.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

A vanishing sum makes the two roots opposites, and the axis of symmetry is always the half-sum of the roots.

$$S=x_{1}+x_{2}$$

$$S= 0$$

$$x_{2}$$

$$S=-x_{1}$$

$$\text{axis}:\ x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$\text{axis}:\ x=\frac{S}{2}$$

$$\text{axis}:\ x=0$$

The line $x=0$ is the vertical coordinate axis, and the two roots sit symmetrically on either side of it at equal distance.

$$S = 0$$

$$b$$

$$\text{axis}:\ x= 0$$

$$g(x)$$

$$\text{axis}:\ x=ax^{2}+c$$

Both halves of the claim hold together.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Arithmetic is unavailable here: the coefficients stay symbolic, so the axis formula has to be argued with rather than evaluated.

$$
x = -\frac{b}{2a},\qquad S = -\frac{b}{a},\qquad P = \frac{c}{a}
$$

The axis of symmetry sits at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, so it follows the first two coefficients and ignores the constant term entirely. Vieta's relations turn the coefficients into the sum and the product of the roots without solving any equation. The discriminant counts the real roots: two while it is positive, one when it vanishes and none once it turns negative.

title: Sliding a Line Until It Touches
context: A fixed parabola $g(x)=x^{2}-2x-5$ is compared with the family of slope-one lines $f_c(x)=x+c$, where $c$ runs through $\mathbb{R}$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: There is exactly one value of $c$ for which the line touches the parabola at a single point.
When the line passes through the origin, it meets the parabola twice.
For every real $c$ the line meets the parabola.
All the lines of the family have the same slope.
Whatever $c$ is, the graphs meet at no more than two points.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The family slides a line of fixed slope up and down, and touching means $g(x)=f_{c}(x)$ has a repeated solution, so form the difference and watch its discriminant.

$$x^{2}-2x-5-(x+c)=x^{2}-3x-(5+c)$$

$$x^{2}-2x-5-(x+c)=0$$

$$\Delta(c)=9+4(5+c)$$

$$\Delta(c)=29+4c$$

This is a first-degree expression in the parameter, so it vanishes for one single value.

$$29+4c = 0$$

$$c$$

$$\Delta(c)=-\frac{29}{4}$$

Exactly one member of the family touches the parabola.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Passing through the origin fixes the parameter, since the intercept of $f_{c}$ is $c$ itself.

$$f_{c}(0)=c$$

$$f_{c}(0)= 0$$

$$f_{0}(x)$$

$$f_{c}(0)=x$$

Now count the solutions of the difference at that parameter value.

$$\Delta(0)=29$$

$$29>0$$

A positive discriminant makes the square root a genuine positive number, so the two abscissas $\frac{3\pm\sqrt{29}}{2}$ are real and different.

The line through the origin cuts the parabola twice.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Whether a member meets the parabola is decided by the sign of the same discriminant, now read as a function of the shift.

$$\Delta(c)=29+4c$$

$$c<-\frac{29}{4}$$

$$\Delta(c)<0$$

Taking $c=-10$, for instance, gives a negative value

$$\Delta(c)=\Delta(-10)$$

$$\Delta(c)=29-40$$

$$\Delta(c)=-11$$

$$-11<0$$

With no real solution left the line has slid too far down and shares no point with the curve.

Sufficiently low members of the family miss the parabola entirely.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The parameter enters $f_{c}$ only as an added constant, so it never touches the coefficient of $x$.

$$f_{c}(x)=x+c$$

$$f_{c}(x_{2})-f_{c}(x_{1})=x_{2}-x_{1}$$

The rate of change is $1$ for every $c$, so all the members are parallel and the whole family is just one line sliding vertically.

Every line of the family has slope one.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The common abscissas are the real roots of the difference, so look at what kind of equation that difference gives.

$$g(x)-f_{c}(x)=x^{2}-3x-(5+c)$$

The parameter only shifts the constant term; the coefficient of $x^{2}$ stays $1$ for every $c$, so the equation remains quadratic.

$$\text{leading coefficient}=1\neq 0$$

$$\text{at most two real roots}$$

Depending on the sign of the discriminant the count is two, one or none, but it can never be three.

Two meetings is the maximum, whatever the shift.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
A fixed parabola $g(x)=x^{2}-2x-5$ is compared with the family of slope-one lines $f_c(x)=x+c$, where $c$ runs through $\mathbb{R}$.

Recover the shared line and parabola once here; each letter only checks the extra arithmetic named in its claim.

$g-f_c=x^{2}-3x-(5+c)$ with discriminant $29+4c$: two meetings, one, or none.

$$
x^{2}-2x-5-(x+c) = x^{2}-3x-(5+c) = 0
$$

$$
\Delta(c) = 9+4(5+c) = 29+4c
$$

$$
29+4c = 0\implies c = -\frac{29}{4}
$$

title: Choosing the Leading Coefficient
context: A one-parameter family of parabolas $g_a(x)=ax^{2}+2x-3$ with $a\neq 0$ is compared with the fixed line $f(x)=x+1$. Consider what the real parameter $a$ can do. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: There is a value of $a$ for which the line is tangent to the parabola.
For every $a\neq 0$ the graphs meet at two distinct points.
Some choice of $a$ makes the graphs miss each other entirely.
The axis of symmetry of $g_a$ is the same for all admissible $a$.
Every parabola of the family crosses the $y$-axis at the same point.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Here the parameter is the leading coefficient itself, so form the difference and treat its discriminant as a function of $a$.

$$ax^{2}+2x-3-(x+1)=ax^{2}+x-4$$

$$ax^{2}+2x-3-(x+1)=0$$

$$\Delta(a)=1+16a$$

Tangency asks for a repeated root, that is a vanishing discriminant, which is a first-degree condition on the parameter.

$$1+16a = 0$$

$$a$$

$$\Delta(a)=-\frac{1}{16}$$

This value is real and non-zero, so it is an admissible member of the family.

One parabola of the family touches the line.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Two distinct meetings require a strictly positive discriminant, so check whether $\Delta(a)=1+16a$ holds for every admissible parameter.

$$\Delta(a)=1+16a$$

$$a<-\frac{1}{16}$$

$$\Delta(a)<0$$

Taking $a=-1$ gives

$$\Delta(a)=\Delta(-1)$$

$$\Delta(a)=1-16$$

$$\Delta(a)=-15$$

$$-15<0$$

so that member has no real meeting abscissa at all.

Sufficiently negative leading coefficients destroy both intersections.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Missing each other is the case of a negative discriminant, and the discriminant moves along a straight line as the parameter varies.

$$\Delta(a)=1+16a$$

$$1+16a<0$$

$$a<-\frac{1}{16}$$

Any parameter below that threshold works; with $a=-1$ the difference has no real root.

$$-x^{2}+x-4 = 0$$

$$
\Delta=1-16 = -15<0
$$

The corresponding parabola opens downwards and stays entirely below the line.

Such a choice of the leading coefficient exists.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The axis of a parabola is computed from its first two coefficients, and here only the leading one carries the parameter $a$.

$$x=-\frac{2}{2a}$$

$$x=-\frac{1}{a}$$

The result depends on $a$, so different members have different axes.

$$a = 1$$

$$x$$

$$x=-1$$

$$a=2$$

$$a=-\frac{1}{2}$$

The axis slides as the leading coefficient changes.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The crossing with the vertical coordinate axis is the value at $x=0$, and the parameter multiplies $x^{2}$, which vanishes there.

$$g_{a}(0)=a\cdot 0+2\cdot 0-3$$

$$g_{a}(0)=-3$$

So every member of the family reaches the same height at $x=0$, however large or small the leading coefficient is.

$$a = 1$$

$$g_{1}(0)$$

$$g_{a}(0)=-3$$

$$a=-5$$

$$h=g_{-5}(0)$$

$$h=-3$$

The whole family therefore pivots through the single point $(0,-3)$.

All of them cross the $y$-axis at that same point.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
A one-parameter family of parabolas $g_a(x)=ax^{2}+2x-3$ with $a\neq 0$ is compared with the fixed line $f(x)=x+1$.

Recover the shared line and parabola once here; each letter only checks the extra arithmetic named in its claim.

$g_a-f=ax^{2}+x-4$ with discriminant $1+16a$; all curves pass through $(0,-3)$.

$$
ax^{2}+2x-3-(x+1) = ax^{2}+x-4 = 0
$$

$$\Delta(a)=1+16a$$

$$
1+16a = 0\implies a = -\frac{1}{16}
$$

title: Coefficient Match Against a Composition
context: Read the line $f(x)=5x+1$ and the parabola $g(x)=3x^{2}-2x-1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Matching $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ forces $A=\frac{3}{25}$.
Matching $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ forces $B=-2$.
The highest power of $x$ in the nested function $f(g(x))$ is $x^{2}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write $g=Af^{2}+Bf+C$ with the given line $f(x)=5x+1$. Only the first summand can create an $x^{2}$ term, and squaring the line contributes $25x^{2}$.

$$A\cdot 5^{2}=3$$

$$A=\frac{3}{25}$$

The division is legitimate because the slope $5$ is non-zero, and no other value of $A$ can reproduce the leading coefficient $3$ of $g$.

Matching forces $A=\frac{3}{25}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

With $A=\frac{3}{25}$ already forced by the $x^{2}$ terms, equate the coefficients of $x$ in $A(5x+1)^{2}+B(5x+1)+C$ and in $g(x)=3x^{2}-2x-1$.

$$A(25x^{2}+10x+1)+B(5x+1)+C=3x^{2}-2x-1$$

The coefficient of $x$ on the left is $10A+5B$, and it must equal $-2$.

$$10\cdot\frac{3}{25}+5B = -2$$

$$x=\frac{6}{5}+5B$$

$$x=-2$$

$$B$$

$$A(25x^{2}+10x+1)+B(5x+1)+C=-\frac{16}{25}$$

The forced value is $-\frac{16}{25}$, not the claimed $-2$.

Matching does not force $B=-2$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Applying the line to the parabola multiplies the parabola by the slope and then adds the intercept, so no new power of $x$ can be created.

$$f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)=5(3x^{2}-2x-1)+1$$

Expanding the bracket keeps the highest power exactly where it was.

$$f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)=15x^{2}-10x-4$$

The highest power is $x^{2}$ with coefficient $15\neq 0$.

The nested function is again a parabola.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

A nested value is computed from the inside outwards: evaluate the inner function at the given number first, then feed the result into the outer function.

$$f(0)=5\cdot 0+1$$

$$f(0)=1$$

That output now becomes the input of $g$.

$$g(1)=3\cdot 1^{2}-2\cdot 1-1$$

$$1^{2}=1$$

$$g(1)=3\cdot 1-2\cdot 1-1$$

$$g(1)=0$$

The nested value is $0$.

$g(f(0))=0$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Nesting is not symmetric: feeding the line into the parabola need not agree with feeding the parabola into the line, so each order has to be computed on its own.

$$g(0)=-1$$

$$f(-1)=5\cdot(-1)+1$$

$$f(-1)=-4$$

$$f(0)=1$$

$$g(1)=3-2-1$$

$$g(1)=3-2$$

$$g(1)=1$$

$$g(1)=1-1$$

$$g(1)=0$$

The two orders give $-4$ and $0$, which are different numbers.

$f(g(0))\neq g(f(0))$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Both rules are handed over with numbers already in place:

$$
f(x) = 5 x + 1,\qquad g(x) = 3 x^{2} - 2 x - 1
$$

Rewriting $g$ as $a(x-h)^{2}+k$ exposes the vertex, with $h$ taken from the axis formula and $k$ obtained by substituting that abscissa back in.

$$
g(x) = 3\left(x-\frac{1}{3}\right)^{2}-\frac{4}{3},\qquad \text{vertex} = \left(\frac{1}{3},-\frac{4}{3}\right)
$$

Because $f$ is a line with non-zero slope, the square $f(x)^{2}$ already carries an $x^{2}$ term, so $g$ can be rebuilt from $f(x)^{2}$, $f(x)$ and a constant. Matching coefficients gives

$$
A = \frac{3}{25},\qquad B = -\frac{16}{25},\qquad C = -\frac{12}{25}
$$

title: Root Spacing Against the Axis of a Parabola
context: The parabola $p$ is given by $p(x)=x^{2}+3x-40$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The distance between the two roots of $p$ is $13$.
The axis of symmetry of $p$ is the line $x=-\frac{3}{2}$.
The two roots of $p$ add up to $3$.
The two roots of $p$ multiply to $-40$.
$p$ is increasing for every $x>-2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The two roots sit symmetrically on either side of the axis, so their gap is $\sqrt{\Delta}/|a|$. Compute the discriminant of the given parabola first.

$$\Delta=3^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot(-40)$$

$$3^{2}=9$$

$$\Delta=9-4\cdot 1\cdot(-40)$$

$$\Delta=9+160$$

$$\Delta=169$$

$$|x_{1}-x_{2}|=\frac{\sqrt{169}}{1}$$

$$|x_{1}-x_{2}|=13$$

Solving $x^{2}+3x-40=0$ recovers the roots $-8$ and $5$, which are indeed $13$ apart.

The distance between the two roots is $13$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Build the axis from the first two coefficients of the given parabola; the constant $-40$ never enters this formula.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+3x-40$$

$$a=1,\ b$$

$$a=3$$

$$x=-\frac{3}{2\cdot 1}$$

$$x=-\frac{3}{2}$$

The graph is symmetric in that vertical line, which is also the midpoint of the roots $-8$ and $5$.

The axis is $x=-\frac{3}{2}$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The sum of the two roots is minus the middle coefficient divided by the leading one.

$$S=-\frac{b}{a}$$

$$S=-\frac{3}{1}$$

$$S=-3$$

The roots themselves are $-8$ and $5$:

$$S=-8+5$$

The claim reports $3$, which drops the minus sign in $-\frac{b}{a}$. The sum is $-3$, not $3$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The product of the two roots is the constant term divided by the leading coefficient.

$$P=\frac{c}{a}$$

$$P=\frac{-40}{1}$$

$$P=-40$$

Multiplying the roots confirms the value:

$$P=(-8)\cdot 5$$

The claim reports exactly this product. The two roots multiply to $-40$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

A parabola changes direction exactly once, at its axis $x=-\frac{3}{2}$.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+3x-40$$

$$a=1$$

$$1>0$$

With a positive stretch the graph falls on everything to the left of the axis and rises on everything to its right.

The half-line $x>-2$ reaches across the axis $x=-\frac{3}{2}$, where the direction changes: on $-2<x<-\frac{3}{2}$ the function is still decreasing.

The claimed half-line is not entirely on the increasing side.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
There is one graph to study, and it is a parabola.

$$p(x)=x^{2}+3x-40$$

The axis formula fixes the turning point, while the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots come out of the coefficients with no equation to solve.

$$
\text{vertex} = \left(-\frac{3}{2},-\frac{169}{4}\right),\qquad S = -3,\qquad P = -40
$$

The discriminant comes out positive, so the graph cuts the $x$-axis twice, once on either side of the axis of symmetry.

$$
\Delta = 169,\qquad x_{1} = -8,\qquad x_{2} = 5
$$

The arms open upwards, so the turning point is the lowest point of the graph and the smallest value is $-\frac{169}{4}$.

title: A Translation Cannot Flatten a Parabola
context: The following pair is given: the line $f(x)=-6x+4$ together with the parabola $g(x)=2x^{2}+3x-2$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Completing the square gives $g(x)=2\left(x+\frac{3}{4}\right)^{2}-\frac{25}{8}$.
Some vertical translation of $g$ makes $f-g$ a constant function.
The vertex of the graph of $g$ is $\left(-\frac{3}{4},-\frac{25}{8}\right)$.
The average rate of change of $g$ on $[0,2]$ equals the slope of $y=f(x)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Completing the square starts from the axis $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$ and the height there.

$$g(x)=2x^{2}+3x-2$$

$$x=-\frac{3}{2\cdot 2}$$

$$x=-\frac{3}{4}$$

$$g\bigl(-\tfrac{3}{4}\bigr)=2\cdot\tfrac{9}{16}+3\cdot\bigl(-\tfrac{3}{4}\bigr)-2$$
