$$g\bigl(-\tfrac{3}{4}\bigr)=\tfrac{9}{8}-\tfrac{9}{4}-2$$

$$g\bigl(-\tfrac{3}{4}\bigr)=-\tfrac{25}{8}$$

Putting the stretch, the shift and the height together recovers the completed square.

$$g(x)=2\bigl(x+\tfrac{3}{4}\bigr)^{2}-\tfrac{25}{8}$$

That is the displayed expression.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Translating a graph vertically adds a fixed number to its formula, which changes the constant term and nothing else, so the $x^{2}$ term of the difference survives untouched.

$$f(x)-g(x)=-2x^{2}-9x+6$$

Shifting $g$ by any real $t$ replaces $g$ by $g+t$ in that difference.

$$f(x)-(g(x)+t)=-2x^{2}-9x+(6-t)$$

The coefficient of $x^{2}$ stays $-2$ for every shift $t$, so the difference remains a genuine parabola and never flattens out.

No vertical translation makes $f-g$ constant.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The turning point sits on the axis just computed, so its height is the value of $g$ there.

$$x=-\frac{3}{4}$$

$$g\bigl(-\tfrac{3}{4}\bigr)=-\tfrac{25}{8}$$

$$\text{vertex}=\bigl(-\tfrac{3}{4},-\tfrac{25}{8}\bigr)$$

The leading coefficient $2$ is positive, so this point is the lowest on the graph.

The vertex is $\bigl(-\frac{3}{4},-\frac{25}{8}\bigr)$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The average rate of change over an interval is the slope of the chord joining the two endpoint values, so evaluate $g$ at both ends.

$$g(0)=-2$$

$$g(2)=8+6-2$$

$$g(2)=8+6$$

$$g(2)=14$$

$$g(2)=14-2$$

$$g(2)=12$$

$$\frac{g(2)-g(0)}{2-0}=\frac{12-(-2)}{2}$$

$$\frac{g(2)-g(0)}{2-0}=7$$

The line $f(x)=-6x+4$ has slope $-6$, which is a different number.

The chord slope $7$ is not the slope of $f$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

A nested value is computed from the inside outwards: evaluate $g(x)=2x^{2}+3x-2$ at $0$ first, then feed the result into $f(x)=-6x+4$.

$$g(0)=2\cdot 0^{2}+3\cdot 0-2$$

$$0^{2}=0$$

$$g(0)=2\cdot 0+3\cdot 0-2$$

$$g(0)=-2$$

That output now becomes the input of the line.

$$f(-2)=-6\cdot(-2)+4$$

$$f(-2)=12+4$$

$$f(-2)=16$$

The nested value is $16$.

$f(g(0))=16$.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Everything starts from the two concrete rules

$$
f(x) = 4 - 6 x,\qquad g(x) = 2 x^{2} + 3 x - 2
$$

The slope, the vertical intercepts and the opening direction all sit in plain view in the coefficients; the arms go upwards.

$$
m = -6,\qquad f(0) = 4,\qquad g(0) = -2,\qquad a = 2
$$

Completing the square moves the turning point of the parabola into view: the axis comes from the first two coefficients and the height is the value of $g$ there.

$$
g(x) = 2\left(x+\frac{3}{4}\right)^{2}-\frac{25}{8},\qquad \text{vertex} = \left(-\frac{3}{4},-\frac{25}{8}\right)
$$

Comparing the two graphs means solving $f(x)=g(x)$, a quadratic equation whose discriminant reports two real solutions.

$$
f(x)-g(x) = - 2 x^{2} - 9 x + 6,\qquad \Delta = 129
$$

title: Lines Through the Vertex
context: A parabola $g$ has vertex $V$ and nonzero leading coefficient $a$. A line $f$ of slope $m$ is drawn through that same vertex. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $m$ vanishes, then $V$ is the only common point of the two graphs.
If $m$ is nonzero, then the graphs have a second common point different from $V$.
Whatever $m$ is, the two graphs are tangent at $V$.
The two graphs always have at least one common point.
When a second common point exists, it lies to the right of the axis of $g$ exactly when $m$ and $a$ have the same sign.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Put the parabola in vertex form around $V=(h,k)$; a line of slope zero through $V$ is simply the horizontal line at that height.

$$g(x)=a(x-h)^{2}+k$$

$$f(x)=k$$

The difference is then a pure square, so the meeting condition has a repeated solution and no other.

$$g(x)-f(x)=a(x-h)^{2}$$

$$g(x)-f(x)= 0$$

$$x$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=h$$

Away from $x=h$ the square is strictly positive and $a\neq 0$, so the difference never returns to zero.

The vertex is the one and only common point in that case.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A line through the vertex can be written using the same shifted variable, and then the difference factors by hand.

$$f(x)=m(x-h)+k$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=a(x-h)^{2}-m(x-h)$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=(x-h)\bigl(a(x-h)-m\bigr)$$

The first factor gives back the vertex; the second one vanishes at an abscissa obtained by dividing the slope by the leading coefficient.

$$a(x-h) = m$$

$$x$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=h+\frac{m}{a}$$

Because $m\neq 0$ and $a\neq 0$ the shift $m/a$ is non-zero, so this second abscissa really is different from $h$.

A second common point appears as soon as the line is tilted.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Tangency would mean the factored difference has a repeated root at the vertex, so look at the factorisation once more.

$$g(x)-f(x)=(x-h)\bigl(a(x-h)-m\bigr)$$

For $m\neq 0$ the factor $x-h$ occurs only once, so the difference changes sign at $x=h$ and the graphs cross there instead of touching.

$$g(x)=x^{2},\ f(x)$$

$$g(x)= x$$

$$g(x)=g(x)-f(x)$$

$$g(x)=x(x-1)$$

In this example the line through the vertex $(0,0)$ cuts the parabola again at $x=1$, and near the origin the difference is negative on one side and positive on the other.

Only the horizontal choice $m=0$ produces a genuine tangency.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The line is required to pass through the vertex, so one common point is handed over by the hypothesis itself.

$$f(h)=k$$

$$f(h)=g(h)$$

Both graphs therefore contain the point $V=(h,k)$, whatever the slope $m$ and the leading coefficient $a$ happen to be.

$$g(x)-f(x)=(x-h)\bigl(a(x-h)-m\bigr)$$

Algebraically the factor $x-h$ is always present in the difference, so the meeting can never be lost.

At least the vertex is always shared.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The second meeting was located exactly, so its position relative to the axis $x=h$ is a matter of one sign.

$$x_{2}=h+\frac{m}{a}$$

$$x_{2}>h$$

$$\frac{m}{a}>0$$

$$m\text{ and }a\text{ have the same sign}$$

solution_overview:
Everything is stated for a general parabola, so the reasoning runs on the structure of $ax^{2}+bx+c$ instead of on numbers.

$$

title: Composing a Parabola With Itself
context: A non-constant line $f$ and a parabola $g$ are given. Consider the nested functions $g(g(x))$ and $g(f(g(x)))$. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The highest power of $x$ in $g(g(x))$ is $x^{4}$.
The highest power of $x$ in $g(f(g(x)))$ is $x^{4}$.
The highest power of $x$ in $g(g(x))$ is $x^{4}$ because the two powers are added rather than multiplied.
The nested function $f(f(x))$ is again a non-constant linear function.
For a suitable $g$, the nested function $g(g(x))$ is a quadratic function.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ with $a\neq 0$. Nesting substitutes the whole parabola in place of $x$, so the square term gets squared and that is where the top power comes from.

$$g\bigl(g(x)\bigr)=a(ax^{2}+bx+c)^{2}+b(ax^{2}+bx+c)+c$$

Squaring an expression whose highest power is $x^{2}$ reaches $x^{4}$, with a coefficient that is a product of non-zero numbers.

$$a(ax^{2})^{2}=a^{3}x^{4}$$

The remaining summands only climb to $x^{2}$, so nothing can cancel the $a^{3}x^{4}$ term.

The highest power really is $x^{4}$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Write $f(x)=mx+q$ with $m\neq 0$. Work from the inside out: applying the line to the parabola only rescales it, and then the outer parabola squares the result.

$$f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)=m(ax^{2}+bx+c)+q$$

The leading coefficient here is $ma$, non-zero because the line is non-constant, so the middle stage is still a parabola.

$$g\bigl(f(g(x))\bigr)=a(ma\,x^{2}+\cdots)^{2}+\cdots$$

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{4}=a(ma)^{2}$$

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{4}= a^{3}m^{2}\neq 0$$

The triple nesting also tops out at $x^{4}$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The value $x^{4}$ is right, but the reason offered is not: powers of nested functions multiply, and here $2$ times $2$ happens to agree with $2$ plus $2$.

$$
2\cdot 2=4,\qquad 2+2 = 4
$$

A single case where the two rules disagree exposes which one is at work: nest the parabola inside the line and count.

$$g\bigl(f(x)\bigr)=a(mx+q)^{2}+b(mx+q)+c$$

The highest power is $x^{2}$, which is $2\cdot 1=2$, not $2+1=3$. Adding the powers is the rule for multiplying two formulas together, not for nesting one inside the other.

The stated justification is the wrong rule, even though the number it produces here is right.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Write $f(x)=mx+q$ with $m\neq 0$. Nesting a line inside itself substitutes a first-degree expression into a first-degree formula, so expand and collect.

$$f\bigl(f(x)\bigr)=m(mx+q)+q$$

$$f\bigl(f(x)\bigr)=m^{2}x+q(m+1)$$

The new slope is $m^{2}$, and a square of a non-zero number is non-zero, so the result is a line that is not constant.

$$m\neq 0$$

$$m^{2}>0$$

The double nesting stays a non-constant line.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

For the nesting to collapse to a parabola, the $x^{4}$ term would have to disappear, so look at the coefficient it carries.

$$g\bigl(g(x)\bigr)=a(ax^{2}+bx+c)^{2}+b(ax^{2}+bx+c)+c$$

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{4}=a^{3}$$

This vanishes only when $a=0$, which is forbidden because $g$ is a parabola; no choice of $b$ or $c$ has any influence on it.

$$a\neq 0$$

$$a^{3}\neq 0$$

The $x^{4}$ term is always there, so the nesting is never a quadratic function.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
No numbers appear, so the claims are settled by what nesting does to the highest power of $x$.

$$
f(x) = mx+q,\qquad g(x) = ax^{2}+bx+c,\quad a\neq 0
$$

Nesting multiplies the highest powers instead of adding them, so feeding a parabola into a parabola reaches $x^{4}$, and inserting a line between them changes nothing about that.

title: Can a Line Trap a Parabola?
context: A parabola $g$ with nonzero leading coefficient $a$ is given together with a line $f$. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $a$ is positive, some line lies strictly below the whole graph of $g$.
If $a$ is positive, some line lies strictly above the whole graph of $g$.
If $a$ is positive, then $g-f$ attains a smallest value for every linear $f$.
If $a$ is negative, some horizontal line lies strictly above the whole graph of $g$.
The graph of $g$ can be squeezed between two distinct parallel lines over all of $\mathbb{R}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

An upward-opening parabola has a lowest point, and any level below that height gives a line the graph never reaches.

$$g(x)=a(x-h)^{2}+k\ge k\quad\text{for all }x,\qquad a>0$$

Take the horizontal line one unit under the vertex; it is a perfectly legitimate linear function.

$$f(x)=k-1$$

$$g(x)-f(x)\ge 1>0$$

The gap between the two graphs is at least one unit everywhere, so the line stays strictly below the parabola.

Such a line exists, for instance that horizontal one.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

A line above the whole graph would need $g(x)<f(x)$ for every $x$, so examine the difference far from the origin.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q),\quad a>0$$

The difference is itself an upward-opening parabola, so it has a lowest point and then climbs beyond every bound on both sides.

$$g(x)-f(x)>0\text{ for all }|x|\text{ large enough}$$

The arms of the parabola therefore rise past any line eventually, no matter how steep the line is chosen.

No line can stay above the whole graph when $a>0$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Subtracting a line changes only the $x$ term and the constant term, so the difference keeps the leading coefficient of $g$.

$$g(x)-f(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q),\quad a>0$$

Completing the square exhibits a non-negative square multiplied by a positive number, plus a constant that is actually attained at the vertex.

$$g(x)-f(x)=a(x-h_{d})^{2}+k_{d}\ge k_{d}$$

The value $k_{d}$ depends on the line chosen, but for each line it is a genuine number reached at one abscissa.

The difference attains a smallest value for every linear $f$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

A negative leading coefficient turns the arms downwards, so the vertex is now the highest point of the graph.

$$g(x)=a(x-h)^{2}+k\le k\quad\text{for all }x,\qquad a<0$$

The square is non-negative and $a<0$, so the product is at most zero and the values never climb past the vertex height $k$.

$$f(x)=k+1$$

$$f(x)-g(x)\ge 1>0$$

The horizontal line one unit above the vertex therefore misses the graph entirely and stays above it.

Such a horizontal line exists.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

A strip between two parallel lines has bounded width, so being squeezed inside it would keep the difference to one of those lines bounded.

$$f_{1}(x)=mx+q_{1}$$

$$f_{2}(x)=mx+q_{2}$$

Subtracting the lower line from $g$ leaves a parabola with the same leading coefficient $a\neq 0$, and such a difference is unbounded.

$$g(x)-f_{1}(x)=ax^{2}+(b-m)x+(c-q_{1})$$

For $a>0$ its values exceed $q_{2}-q_{1}$ once $|x|$ is large, and for $a<0$ they fall below the strip instead, so the graph escapes on one side or the other.

A parabola always breaks out of a strip of finite width.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The parabola arrives already centred on its vertex, so the reasoning stays with the roles of $a$, $h$ and $k$.

$$g(x)=a\left(x-h\right)^{2}+k$$

Completed-square form puts the turning point at $(h,k)$, and the sign of $a$ decides whether $k$ is the smallest or the largest value taken. Far out on either side the $x^{2}$ term outgrows every linear term, so the parabola decides who ends up on top.

title: Reading Roots Through a Linear Substitution
context: A non-constant line $f$ has slope $m$, and an outer parabola is written $q(y)=Ay^{2}+By+C$ with nonzero $A$. Set $g(x)=q(f(x))$. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The function $g$ is a quadratic function.
Every real root of $g$ is a point at which $f$ takes a root value of $q$.
If $q$ has no real roots, then $g$ has no real roots.
The roots of $g$ coincide with the roots of $q$.
The coefficient of $x^{2}$ in $g$ equals $A$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write $f(x)=mx+k$ with $m\neq 0$. Substituting the line into the outer formula replaces $y$ by a first-degree expression, so expand and collect the powers of $x$.

$$g(x)=A(mx+k)^{2}+B(mx+k)+C$$

$$g(x)=Am^{2}x^{2}+(2Amk+Bm)x+(Ak^{2}+Bk+C)$$

The coefficient of $x^{2}$ is the product $Am^{2}$, and both factors are non-zero: $A$ by hypothesis and $m$ because the line is non-constant.

The substitution produces a genuine quadratic function.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The composite is evaluated in two stages, so a zero of the whole thing is a zero produced at the second stage.

$$g(x_{0})=q\bigl(f(x_{0})\bigr)$$

If this number is zero then the value $y_{0}=f(x_{0})$ satisfies $q(y_{0})=0$, so it is one of the roots of $q$.

$$g(x_{0}) = 0$$

$$q(y_{0})$$

$$y_{0}=f(x_{0})$$

The reasoning uses nothing but the definition of nesting, so it applies to every real root of $g$.

Each root of the composite is an abscissa where the line hits a root of $q$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The composite can only reach values that $q$ itself takes, so a $q$ that never vanishes hands its property straight over.

$$q(y)\neq 0\text{ for every real }y$$

For any real $x$ the number $f(x)$ is real, so $q$ evaluated there is non-zero as well.

$$g(x)=q\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\neq 0\quad\text{for all real }x$$

In terms of discriminants, $q$ having none means its graph misses the horizontal axis, and substituting a line cannot pull it back down.

The composite has no real roots either.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The roots of the composite are the abscissas whose image under $f$ is a root of $q$, so they are the roots of $q$ pulled back through the line.

$$g(x)=0$$

$$f(x)\text{ is a root of }q$$

One concrete pair shows the shift at once.

$$f(x)=x+1$$

$$q(y)=y^{2}$$

$$g(x)$$

$$q(y)=(x+1)^{2}$$

The only root of $q$ is $0$, while the only root of $g$ is $-1$, so the two sets do not coincide.

The line moves the roots unless it happens to be the identity.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The expansion already displays the leading coefficient of the composite, and the slope of the line is squared into it.

$$g(x)=Am^{2}x^{2}+(2Amk+Bm)x+(Ak^{2}+Bk+C)$$

So the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is $Am^{2}$, which equals $A$ only in the special case $m^{2}=1$.

$$m = 2$$

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{2}$$

$$g(x)= 4A\neq A\text{ unless }A$$

$$g(x)=0$$

Since $A\neq 0$ is assumed, a slope such as $m=2$ genuinely changes the number in front of $x^{2}$.

The leading coefficient is $Am^{2}$, not $A$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Nothing is numeric here, so the sign of the discriminant is the only lever available.

$$\Delta=b^{2}-4ac$$

The discriminant counts the real roots: two while it is positive, one when it vanishes and none once it turns negative.

The parabola arrives as a second function wrapped around a line, so the substitution has to be unwound before the roots can be read.

title: Equal Values and the Axis
context: A parabola $g$ has nonzero leading coefficient and axis of symmetry $\ell$. Two distinct real numbers $u$ and $v$ satisfy $g(u)=g(v)$. No numeric data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The line $\ell$ passes through the midpoint of $u$ and $v$.
The numbers $u$ and $v$ must be the roots of $g$.
For every positive real $t$, the two points at distance $t$ from $\ell$ on either side carry equal values of $g$.
The sum $u+v$ is determined by the coefficients of $g$ alone.
Such a pair of distinct numbers with equal values exists for every quadratic $g$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Write $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$ with $a\neq 0$. Two equal values give an equation between the coefficients, so subtract the two evaluations and factor.

$$g(u)-g(v)=a(u^{2}-v^{2})+b(u-v)$$

$$g(u)-g(v)=(u-v)\bigl(a(u+v)+b\bigr)$$

The first factor is non-zero because $u$ and $v$ are distinct, so the second one must vanish, which pins down the sum.

$$a(u+v)+b = 0$$

$$a(u+v)+b=\frac{u+v}{2}$$

$$g(u)-g(v)=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

The right-hand side is exactly the abscissa of the axis of symmetry.

The axis passes through the midpoint of the two abscissas.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Equal values need not be zero values, so nothing forces the common value onto the horizontal axis.

$$g(x)=x^{2}$$

$$u=1$$

$$v=-1$$

$$g(1)=1$$

$$g(1)=g(-1)$$

The hypothesis is satisfied with a common value of $1$, yet the only root of this parabola is $0$, which is neither $u$ nor $v$.

$$g(x) = 0$$

$$x$$

$$g(1)=0$$

Symmetric pairs of abscissas exist at every height, not only at height zero.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Vertex form makes the symmetry visible: only the distance from the axis enters, through a square.

$$g(x)=a(x-h)^{2}+k$$

$$\ell:\ x=h$$

Evaluating at the two abscissas $h+t$ and $h-t$ squares the same number up to sign, so the two results agree.

$$g(h+t)=at^{2}+k$$

$$g(h-t)=at^{2}+k$$

This holds for every positive $t$, and the two abscissas are genuinely different because $t\neq 0$.

Points mirrored in the axis always carry the same value.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Write $g(x)=ax^{2}+bx+c$. The relation derived from $g(u)=g(v)$ involved no data beyond the coefficients, so read it again.

$$(u-v)\bigl(a(u+v)+b\bigr)=0,\quad u\neq v$$

$$u+v=-\frac{b}{a}$$

Whatever pair of distinct abscissas with equal values one starts from, its sum is this one number, which is twice the abscissa of the axis.

The sum is fixed by $a$ and $b$ alone.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The axis of symmetry always exists, and it supplies such a pair for free.

$$h=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$u=h+1$$

$$v=h-1$$

These two numbers are distinct, and vertex form shows they carry the same value.

$$g(h+1)=a+k$$

$$g(h+1)=g(h-1)$$

The construction only needs $a\neq 0$, which is part of being a quadratic function, so it works for every $g$ of this kind.

Such a pair can always be produced.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Arithmetic is unavailable here: the coefficients stay symbolic, so the axis formula has to be argued with rather than evaluated.

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

The axis of symmetry sits at $x=-\frac{b}{2a}$, so it follows the first two coefficients and ignores the constant term entirely.

The axis carries its own name here, and every letter compares it with some other line.

title: A Pencil of Lines and Two Tangents
context: A fixed parabola $g(x)=x^{2}-4x+6$ is compared with the family of lines $f_t(x)=t(x-1)+2$ obtained as the real parameter $t$ varies. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Every line of the family passes through one and the same point.
There are exactly two slopes for which the line touches the parabola at a single point.
There are slopes for which the line misses the parabola completely.
For every slope the line meets the parabola at two distinct points.
The fixed point common to all the lines lies on the parabola.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The parameter multiplies the bracket $x-1$, so it loses all its influence wherever that bracket vanishes.

$$f_{t}(1)=t\cdot 0+2$$

$$f_{t}(1)=2$$

Every member of the family therefore reaches the height $2$ at the abscissa $1$, whatever the slope.

$$t = 0$$

$$f_{0}(x)$$

$$f_{t}(1)=2$$

$$t=3$$

$$f_{3}(x)$$

$$t=3x-1$$

Both of these pass through $(1,2)$, and the same computation works for any slope: the family is a pencil of lines hinged at that point.

One fixed point is common to all the lines.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Touching at a single point means $g(x)=f_{t}(x)$ has a repeated solution, so collect the terms and set the discriminant to zero.

$$x^{2}-4x+6-t(x-1)-2=x^{2}-(4+t)x+(4+t)$$

$$x^{2}-4x+6-t(x-1)-2=0$$

$$\Delta(t)=(4+t)^{2}-4(4+t)$$

$$\Delta(t)=t(4+t)$$

The condition is now a quadratic equation in the slope, and it factors immediately.

$$t(4+t) = 0$$

$$t$$

$$\Delta(t)=0\text{ or }t$$

$$\Delta(t)=-4$$

The first gives the horizontal line $y=2$ touching at the vertex $(2,2)$, the second the line $y=-4x+6$ touching at $(0,6)$.

There are exactly two such slopes.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

A member misses the parabola exactly when the discriminant is negative, so study the sign of the product just obtained.

$$\Delta(t)=t(4+t)$$

A product of two factors is negative when they have opposite signs, which happens strictly between the two roots.

$$-4<t<0$$

$$\Delta(t)<0$$

$$t = -2$$

$$t=\Delta(-2)$$

$$\Delta(t)=(-2)\cdot 2$$

$$\Delta(t)=-4$$

$$-4<0$$

The line $y=-2x+4$ therefore shares no point with the curve.

Slopes in that window make the line miss the parabola.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Two distinct meetings need a strictly positive discriminant, and the discriminant has already been factored.

$$\Delta(t)=t(4+t)$$

It vanishes at $t=0$ and $t=-4$, where the line only touches the curve, and it is negative in between, where nothing is shared.

$$t = -2$$

$$\Delta$$

$$\Delta(t)=-4$$

$$-4<0$$

$$t=0$$

Some slopes give one meeting and some give none, so two distinct meetings do not always occur.

The claim fails for a whole interval of slopes.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The fixed point of the pencil was found to be $(1,2)$, so test whether the parabola reaches that height there.

$$g(1)=1^{2}-4+6$$

$$1^{2}=1$$

$$g(1)=1-4+6$$

$$g(1)=1-4$$

$$g(1)=-3$$

$$g(1)=-3+6$$

$$g(1)=3$$

The parabola is at height $3$ while the fixed point sits at height $2$, so the point lies strictly below the curve.

$$\text{vertex of }g=(2,2),\qquad g(1)=3\neq 2$$

That position is exactly what makes the two tangent lines and the window of missing lines possible.

The hinge point of the family is not on the parabola.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
A fixed parabola $g(x)=x^{2}-4x+6$ is compared with the family of lines $f_t(x)=t(x-1)+2$ obtained as the real parameter $t$ varies.

Recover the shared line and parabola once here; each letter only checks the extra arithmetic named in its claim.

$g-f_t=x^{2}-(4+t)x+(4+t)$ with discriminant $t(4+t)$: two tangent slopes, and no meeting in between.

$$
f_{t}(1) = t\cdot 0+2 = 2
$$

$$
t = 0\implies f_{0}(x) = 2,\qquad t = 3\implies f_{3}(x) = 3x-1
$$

$$
x^{2}-4x+6-t(x-1)-2 = x^{2}-(4+t)x+(4+t) = 0
$$

title: Sliding the Parabola Sideways
context: A fixed line $f(x)=2x-1$ is compared with the family of parabolas $g_r(x)=(x-r)^{2}-4$ obtained as the real shift $r$ varies. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: There is exactly one shift for which the line is tangent to the parabola.
For sufficiently negative shifts the line and the parabola do not meet.
The vertex height of $g_r$ depends on $r$.
The axis of symmetry of $g_r$ moves as $r$ changes.
Every parabola of the family crosses the $y$-axis at the same point.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The family moves a fixed parabola left and right, and tangency means $g_{r}(x)=f(x)$ has a repeated solution.

$$(x-r)^{2}-4-(2x-1)=x^{2}-(2r+2)x+(r^{2}-3)$$

$$(x-r)^{2}-4-(2x-1)=0$$

$$\Delta(r)=(2r+2)^{2}-4(r^{2}-3)$$

$$\Delta(r)=8r+16$$

The squares in $r$ cancel, so the condition is a first-degree equation with one solution.

$$8r+16 = 0$$

$$r$$

$$\Delta(r)=-2$$

At that shift the difference becomes $(x+1)^{2}$, a perfect square touching zero once.

Exactly one shift makes the line tangent.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Missing each other means a negative discriminant, and the discriminant just computed increases steadily with the shift.

$$\Delta(r)=8r+16$$

$$r<-2$$

$$\Delta(r)<0$$

Taking $r=-3$, for instance, leaves no real solution:

$$\Delta(r)=\Delta(-3)$$

$$\Delta(r)=-24+16$$

$$\Delta(r)=-8$$

$$-8<0$$

Pushed far enough to the left, the parabola has slid out from under the rising line and the two curves share nothing.

Sufficiently negative shifts separate the graphs.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The formula is already in vertex form, so the turning point can be read straight off it.

$$g_{r}(x) = (x-r)^{2}-4$$

$$\text{vertex}=(r,-4)$$

The shift appears in the bracket only, which moves the vertex sideways; the constant $-4$ outside the square is the height, and $r$ never enters it.

$$r = 0$$

$$\text{vertex }(0,-4)$$

$$r=5$$

$$\text{vertex }(5,-4)$$

The vertex height stays $-4$ for every shift.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The axis of symmetry is the vertical line through the vertex, and vertex form puts the vertex at abscissa $r$.

$$g_{r}(x) = (x-r)^{2}-4$$

$$\ell:\ x=r$$

The mirrored values confirm it, since only the distance from $r$ enters the square.

$$g_{r}(r+t)=t^{2}-4$$

$$g_{r}(r+t)=g_{r}(r-t)$$

Changing $r$ therefore drags the axis along with the whole graph.

The axis moves exactly as much as the shift.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The crossing with the vertical coordinate axis is the value at $x=0$, so substitute and see whether the shift survives.

$$g_{r}(0)=(0-r)^{2}-4$$

$$g_{r}(0)=r^{2}-4$$

The result depends on $r$, and two members already disagree.

$$r = 0$$

$$g_{0}(0)$$

$$g_{r}(0)=-4$$

$$r=3$$

$$g_{3}(0)$$

$$r=5$$

solution_overview:

title: Rebuild from a Vertex and a Point
context: The line $f$ has slope $-3$ and passes through the point $(1,2)$. The quadratic $g$ has leading coefficient $2$ and its vertex at $(2,-8)$. Recover both formulas, then judge the statements. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

A product vanishes exactly when one of its factors does, and the factor $2$ never does.

$$2x(x-4) = 0$$

$$x$$

$$g(x)=0\text{ or }x$$

$$g(x)=4$$

The midpoint of the two roots is $2$, which is the axis of symmetry found from the vertex, so the two computations agree.

**D.** → False

$$g(0)=0$$

$$2x^{2}-8x = -3x+5$$

$$\Delta=25+40$$

$$x$$

title: Axis Gap, Vieta, and Nested Order
context: A concrete line $f$ and a concrete parabola $g$ are supplied: $f(x)=3x-7$, $g(x)=x^{2}-5x+2$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Completing the square gives $g(x)=\left(x-\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{17}{4}$.
At the axis of $g$ the gap $f-g$ equals $\frac{19}{4}$.
By Vieta the sum of the roots of $g$ is $-5$.
The graphs of $f$ and $g$ meet at two distinct points.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Completing the square isolates the axis shift from half the middle coefficient, then restores the constant so the rewritten formula matches the original polynomial.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-5x+2$$

Halve the middle coefficient of the monic quadratic factor.

$$\frac{b}{2a}=-\frac{5}{2}$$

$$\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2=\frac{25}{4}$$

The axis shift is the opposite of that half-coefficient.

$$h=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$h=\frac{5}{2}$$

Evaluate the original rule at the axis to read the completed-square height.

$$g\left(\frac{5}{2}\right)=-\frac{17}{4}$$

Assemble the stretch, the shift, and the height.

$$g(x)=\left(x-\frac{5}{2}\right)^2-\frac{17}{4}$$

That matches the claimed completed-square form.

$$g(x)=\left(x-\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{17}{4}$$

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The vertical gap between the two graphs at a given abscissa is the difference of the two heights there, so locate the axis of the parabola first and then evaluate both models on it.

$$x=\frac{5}{2}$$

$$f\bigl(\tfrac{5}{2}\bigr)=3\cdot\tfrac{5}{2}-7$$

$$f\bigl(\tfrac{5}{2}\bigr)=\tfrac{1}{2}$$

$$g\bigl(\tfrac{5}{2}\bigr)=-\tfrac{17}{4}$$

Subtracting the parabola height from the line height gives the gap.

$$\tfrac{1}{2}-\bigl(-\tfrac{17}{4}\bigr)=\tfrac{2}{4}+\tfrac{17}{4}$$

$$\tfrac{1}{2}-\bigl(-\tfrac{17}{4}\bigr)=\tfrac{19}{4}$$

The gap is $\frac{19}{4}$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The sum of the two roots is minus the middle coefficient divided by the leading one. For $g(x)=x^{2}-5x+2$,

$$S=-\frac{b}{a}$$

$$S=-\frac{-5}{1}$$

$$S=5$$

The claim reports $-5$, which keeps the minus sign in front of $b$ instead of cancelling it against the minus already present in $-5$. The sum of the roots is $5$, not $-5$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Nesting is not symmetric: feeding the line into the parabola need not agree with feeding the parabola into the line, so each order has to be computed on its own.

$$f(0)=-7$$

$$g(-7)=49+35+2$$

$$g(-7)=49+35$$

$$g(-7)=84$$

$$g(-7)=84+2$$

$$g(-7)=86$$

$$g(0)=2$$

$$f(2)=6-7$$

$$f(2)=-1$$

The two orders give $86$ and $-1$, which are different numbers.

$g(f(0))\neq f(g(0))$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The abscissas where the graphs meet solve $g(x)=f(x)$, so bring the line over and read the discriminant.

$$x^{2}-5x+2-(3x-7)=x^{2}-8x+9$$

$$x^{2}-5x+2-(3x-7)=0$$

$$\Delta=(-8)^{2}-4\cdot 1\cdot 9$$

$$\Delta=64-36$$

$$\Delta=28$$

A strictly positive discriminant makes the square root a genuine positive number, so the quadratic formula returns two different real abscissas.

$$x=\frac{8\pm\sqrt{28}}{2}$$

$$x=4\pm\sqrt{7}$$

Both values are real and they differ by $2\sqrt{7}$, so the line cuts the parabola in two separate points.

The graphs meet at two distinct points.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The stem names a line and a parabola,

$$
f(x) = 3 x - 7,\qquad g(x) = x^{2} - 5 x + 2
$$

The turning point is worth having in hand: the axis of symmetry is read off the first two coefficients, and evaluating $g$ there supplies the height.

$$
g(x) = \left(x-\frac{5}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{17}{4},\qquad \text{vertex} = \left(\frac{5}{2},-\frac{17}{4}\right)
$$

Coefficients alone settle the sum $S$ and the product $P$ of the roots of $g$, and the sign of its discriminant tells how many of those roots are real.

$$
S = 5,\qquad P = 2,\qquad \Delta_{g} = 17
$$

Wherever the two graphs touch, the difference $f-g$ is zero; that difference is quadratic and its discriminant leaves two crossings.

$$
f(x)-g(x) = - x^{2} + 8 x - 9,\qquad \Delta = 28
$$

title: Clearance plot — meetings and a chord
context: The figure shows a **solid brown parabola** $g$ and a **dashed green line** $f$. No formulas are printed. Reason from the ticks, crossings, and relative heights only. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The product of the two meeting abscissas of the graphs is negative.
At the solid curve's turning abscissa the dashed line sits two units above the solid curve.
The two graphs meet exactly once to the left of the origin.
On the open interval between the solid curve's two axis crossings, the solid curve stays below the dashed line.
A chord joining the solid curve's two axis crossings would coincide with the dashed line.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Meetings of a line and a parabola are the real zeros of their height difference, so recover both traces from the ticks and subtract.

$$g(x)=-x^{2}+4$$

$$f(x)=-x+2$$

The difference stays quadratic and factors at sight.

$$g(x)-f(x)=-x^{2}+x+2$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=-(x-2)(x+1)$$

The zeros are $x=-1$ and $x=2$. Their product is already visible from the signs: one meeting sits left of the origin and one sits right of it.

$$P=(-1)\cdot 2$$

$$P=-2$$

A negative product is exactly the claim.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The solid curve turns on the vertical axis, at the unique trough of an even downward parabola. Compare the two heights at that common abscissa.

$$g(x)=-x^{2}+4$$

$$g(0)=4$$

$$f(x)=-x+2$$

$$f(0)=2$$

The dashed line sits two units *below* the solid peak, not above it. The claimed gap runs in the wrong direction.

$$h=4-2$$

$$h=2$$

$$2>0$$

A gap of two units with the wrong sign is the usual mix-up of which trace sits on top at $x=0$.

Green is under brown at the turning abscissa.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Use the shared rules recovered in the overview.

$$g(x)-f(x)=-x^{2}+x+2$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=-(x-2)(x+1)$$

The two real meetings are therefore $x=-1$ and $x=2$. Only the first of those is strictly negative.

$$x=-1$$

$$-1<0$$

$$x=2$$

$$2>0$$

A meeting to the right of the origin does not count toward the left-hand tally, and a quadratic difference has no third real zero.

A single negative abscissa is exactly one meeting to the left of the origin.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The solid curve meets the horizontal axis at $x=\pm 2$. On the open interval between those crossings the midpoint $x=0$ already compares the two traces.

$$g(x)=-x^{2}+4$$

$$f(x)=-x+2$$

$$g(0)=4$$

$$f(0)=2$$

Brown stays above green at the vertex, and an upward gap at the axis of a downward parabola cannot flip between the two roots.

$$4>2$$

The solid curve is above the dashed line on that interval, not below it.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

A chord joining the two axis crossings of $g$ is the unique line through $(\pm 2,0)$, which is the horizontal axis itself.

$$g(\pm 2) = 0$$

$$y=0$$

The dashed trace is a different line: it has slope $-1$ and intercept $2$.

$$f(x)=-x+2$$

The chord of the two roots of $g$ is the $x$-axis for this even downward parabola, while $f$ is a falling line through $(0,2)$.

Those two formulas disagree at every $x\neq 2$. In particular $f(0)=2\neq 0$, so the chord and the dashed trace do not coincide.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The figure prints no formulas, so the first job is to recover both rules from the ticks and the marked points. The solid brown curve peaks on the vertical axis at height $4$ and meets the horizontal axis at $x=\pm 2$; those three facts force a downward unit square.

$$g(x)=-x^{2}+4$$

The dashed green line falls through $(0,2)$ with slope $-1$.

$$f(x)=-x+2$$

The turning point is already sitting in completed-square form: the axis is the vertical coordinate axis and the height there is $4$.

$$
g(x) = 4-x^{2},\qquad \mathrm{ver} = \left(0,4\right)
$$

At that same abscissa the line sits two units lower, so the peak is strictly above the dashed trace.

$$
g(0) = 4,\qquad f(0) = 2

Coefficients of $g$ settle the sum and the product of the roots, and the discriminant confirms that both axis crossings are real.

$$
S = 0,\qquad P = -4,\qquad \Delta_{g} = 16,\qquad x = \pm 2
$$

Common points of the two graphs are the zeros of the quadratic difference; a positive discriminant leaves two meetings.

$$
g(x)-f(x) = -x^{2}+x+2,\qquad \Delta = 9
$$

$$
x = -1,\qquad x = 2

Between those two roots the parabola arches above the axis while the line cuts lower, so on that open interval brown stays above green. The leading coefficient $-1$ sends the arms downwards.

title: Sampled heights — interpolating parabola
context: A sequence $s_n$ is recorded in the table for $n=0,1,2,3,4,5$. No closed form is supplied. Decide each claim from the table alone. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The unique quadratic through the listed points has roots at $n=1$ and $n=3$.
Extending the constant-second-difference pattern one step past $n=5$ produces $s_6=12$.
The axis of that interpolating parabola is $n=2$, the unique listed input of smallest height.
A line matching $s_0$ and $s_5$ also matches $s_2$.
The vertex height of the interpolating parabola equals $-1$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Equally spaced inputs make neighbouring gaps the fastest diagnostic. The first-difference row is not constant, while the second-difference row stands still, so a unique quadratic fits the six points.

$$s:\ 3,\ 0,\ -1,\ 0,\ 3,\ 8$$

$$\Delta_{2}:\ 2,\ 2,\ 2,\ 2$$

For unit spacing that second-difference constant equals $2a$, hence $a=1$. Matching $s_0=3$ and $s_1=0$ then pins the rest.

$$s_n=n^{2}-4n+3$$

$$s_n=(n-1)(n-3)$$

The interpolating parabola vanishes at $n=1$ and $n=3$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The last first-difference of the table is $5$. One further second-difference of $2$ produces the next first-difference $7$, and then the next height.

$$s:\ 3,\ 0,\ -1,\ 0,\ 3,\ 8\qquad \Delta_{1}\text{ last}=5$$

$$s_6=s_5+7$$

$$s_6=8+7$$

$$s_6=15$$

The announced $12$ would have required a first-difference of $4$ instead of $7$.

$$15\neq 12$$

Constant second differences of $2$ force every new first gap to grow by exactly $2$, so the arithmetic cannot jump down to a first gap of $4$.

The extrapolated height is $15$, not $12$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The interpolating parabola through the six cells is $s_n=n^{2}-4n+3$, which factors as $(n-1)(n-3)$. The axis of $an^{2}+bn+c$ is the midpoint of the two roots.

$$n=\frac{1+3}{2}$$

$$n=\frac{4}{2}$$

$$n=2$$

The same abscissa is the unique listed input at which the table attains its smallest height $-1$.

$$s_2=-1\qquad s_n>s_2\text{ for every other listed }n$$

The axis is $n=2$, where the table attains its unique listed minimum.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The unique line through the tabled endpoints $(0,3)$ and $(5,8)$ has slope $1$, so its height at $n=2$ would be $5$.

$$m=\frac{8-3}{5-0}$$

$$m=1$$

$$P=3+2\cdot 1$$

$$P=5$$

The listed height at that same input is $s_2=-1$, which is not $5$. A line matching the two ends therefore misses the middle.

$$s_2=-1\neq 5$$

A chord of the two endpoints is a line, while the table is a genuine parabola, so a mismatch at an interior node is expected.

That line misses the listed height at $n=2$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The vertex of a parabola sits on its axis. Use the shared quadratic recovered in the overview.

$$s_n=n^{2}-4n+3$$

The axis is

$$n=-b/(2a)$$

$$n=2$$

and that column of the table is already the height.

$$s_2=-1$$

For an upward parabola the vertex height is the unique listed minimum, already sitting in the $n=2$ column.

Substituting into the rebuilt rule recovers the same turning height: $4-8+3=-1$. Either way the vertex height equals $-1$.

solution_overview:
The table is the whole stem, so read it as a list of pairs and form the neighbouring gaps; no closed form is printed, but a quadratic can be rebuilt from those gaps.

$$(0,3),\;(1,0),\;(2,-1),\;(3,0),\;(4,3),\;(5,8)$$

The inputs are equally spaced by $1$, which makes the first differences the fastest diagnostic.

$$\mathrm{fir}:\ -3,\ -1,\ 1,\ 3,\ 5$$

Those first gaps themselves change by a constant $2$, the signature of a quadratic sequence rather than a line.

$$\mathrm{sec}:\ 2,\ 2,\ 2,\ 2$$

For unit spacing the second-difference constant equals $2a$, so the leading coefficient is $1$. Matching $s_0=3$ and $s_1=0$ then fixes the remaining two coefficients.

$$
2a = 2,\qquad a = 1
$$

$$s_n=n^{2}-4n+3$$

The rebuilt parabola turns at $n=2$ with height $-1$, and the table is symmetric about that input: $s_0=s_4=3$ and $s_1=s_3=0$. A linear rule is impossible because the first differences are not constant.

$$

$$

title: Meetings, vertex, and a rewrite in $f$
context: Let $f(x)=x+1$ and $g(x)=x^{2}-4x+1$. Work in symbols; no figure is supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The sum of the meeting abscissas of the two graphs equals $5$.
The axis of $g$ is $x=2$, which is half the Vieta sum of the roots of $g$.
The vertex of $g$ lies $3$ units below the horizontal axis.

tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Meetings of a line and a parabola are the real zeros of their difference. Subtract the given line from the given parabola.

$$g(x)-f(x)=(x^{2}-4x+1)-(x+1)$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=x^{2}-5x$$

The difference factors at sight, so the two abscissas are $0$ and $5$. Vieta already reads their sum from the middle coefficient.

$$
x(x-5)=0,\qquad 0+5 = 5
$$

A quadratic difference has at most two real zeros, and both of them appear here, adding to $5$.

The sum of the meeting abscissas is $5$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The axis of $ax^{2}+bx+c$ is the vertical line through $-b/(2a)$, and it ignores the constant term entirely.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-4x+1$$

$$x=-\frac{-4}{2\cdot 1}$$

$$x=-\frac{-4}{2}$$

$$x=2$$

Vieta's sum of the roots is $-b/a=4$, and half of that sum is the same abscissa.

$$\frac{4}{2}$$

$$g(x)=2$$

The constant term $1$ never enters the axis formula, which is why $x=2$ can be read off $a$ and $b$ alone.

$$S=-b/a$$

$$S=4$$

$$x=S/2$$

$$x=2$$

The axis is $x=2$, which is half the Vieta sum of the roots of $g$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The vertex height is the value of $g$ on its axis $x=2$. Substitute that abscissa term by term.

$$g(2)=4-8+1$$

$$g(2)=4-8$$

$$g(2)=-4$$

$$g(2)=-4+1$$

$$g(2)=-3$$

A point of height $-3$ sits three units below the horizontal axis. Completing the square makes the same height visible as the constant beside the square.

$$g(x)=(x-2)^{2}-3$$

A negative vertex height for an upward parabola means the graph dips below the axis between its two real roots.

$$-3<0$$

The vertex lies $3$ units below the axis.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Vieta reads the product of the roots from the constant term over the leading coefficient, without solving.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-4x+1$$

$$P=\frac{c}{a}$$

$$P=1$$

The same number is $g(0)$, because every term with an $x$ dies at the origin.

$$g(0)=1$$

The identity

$$P=c/a$$

$$P=g(0)$$

 holds for every monic quadratic, because only the constant term survives at the origin.

$$g(0)=1$$

$$g(0)=P$$

The product of the roots is $1$, matching $g(0)$.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Because $f$ is a non-constant line, the square $f(x)^{2}$ already carries an $x^{2}$ term, so $1$, $f$ and $f^{2}$ span every parabola. Expand the claimed combination.

$$f(x)^{2}=(x+1)^{2}$$

$$f(x)^{2}=x^{2}+2x+1$$

$$f(x)^{2}-6f(x)+6=x^{2}+2x+1-6(x+1)+6$$

$$f(x)^{2}-6f(x)+6=x^{2}-4x+1$$

Matching coefficients of $x^{2}$, then $x$, then the constant term, is always possible once $f$ is a non-constant line.

$$g(x)=f(x)^{2}-6f(x)+6$$

The combination reproduces $g$ identically, so the claimed rewrite holds.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
Both rules are handed over with numbers already in place.

$$
f(x) = 2x+1,\qquad g(x) = x^{2}-3x+1
$$

The turning point of $g$ is worth having in hand: the axis comes from the first two coefficients, and evaluating $g$ there supplies the height.

Because $f$ is a line with non-zero slope, the square $f(x)^{2}$ already carries an $x^{2}$ term, so $g$ can be rebuilt from $f(x)^{2}$, $f(x)$ and a constant. Matching coefficients gives the triple named in letter E.

title: Sliding slope family — when tangency happens
context: For each real $t$ let $f_t(x)=tx$ and $g(x)=x^{2}+1$. Study how the line family meets the fixed parabola. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Tangency occurs precisely at the two slopes $t=2$ and $t=-2$.
The graphs never miss each other: every real $t$ produces at least one meeting.
For $t=0$ the graphs meet at two real points, because $x^{2}+1$ factors over the reals.
When $t=3$ the graphs miss each other, because $|t|>2$ forces a negative discriminant.
The axis of $g$ depends on $t$, and for $t=0$ that axis coincides with the line $f_0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Tangency is the algebraic statement that the difference has a repeated root, so the discriminant in the slope parameter must vanish.

$$g(x)-f_t(x)=x^{2}-tx+1$$

$$\Delta=t^{2}-4$$

$$\Delta=0$$

$$t=\pm 2$$

Those two slopes, and only those two, make the line touch the parabola. For every other $t$ the discriminant is nonzero, so the root is not repeated.

A repeated root of $x^{2}-tx+1$ is equivalent to the line being the tangent to the parabola at that abscissa.

Tangency occurs precisely at $t=\pm 2$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The same discriminant is negative for every slope strictly between the two tangent values, and a negative discriminant means no real meeting.

$$\Delta=t^{2}-4$$

When $|t|<2$, one has $\Delta<0$.

Take the concrete middle value $t=0$: the difference is $x^{2}+1$, which has no real zero. A miss is therefore possible.

$$x^{2}+1=0\text{ has no real }x$$

The two-meeting range is the complementary region $|t|>2$, where $\Delta>0$. Between the tangents the graphs miss.

The family misses whenever $|t|<2$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

For $t=0$ the line is the horizontal axis, so meetings solve $x^{2}+1=0$.

$$g(x)-f_0(x)=x^{2}+1$$

No real solution exists: a square cannot equal $-1$, so $x^{2}+1$ does not factor over the reals. The graphs share no real point at all, let alone two.

$$x^{2}=-1\text{ is impossible in }\mathbb{R}$$

Completing the square makes the miss visible as $x^{2}+1\ge 1>0$, so the horizontal axis never meets $g$.

There is no real meeting when $t=0$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Substitute the named slope into the discriminant of $x^{2}-tx+1$. The miss range is $|t|<2$, not $|t|>2$.

$$t=3$$

$$\Delta=9-4$$

$$\Delta=5$$

$$5>0$$

A positive discriminant gives two distinct real meetings, not a miss: $|t|>2$ is the two-meeting range.

$$x^{2}-3x+1=0\text{ has two real roots}$$

The sign of $\Delta=t^{2}-4$ flips at the tangent slopes $\pm 2$, so $|t|>2$ is two meetings and $|t|<2$ is a miss.

$$t=3$$

$$3>2$$

$$\text{two real meetings}$$

The graphs meet twice when $t=3$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The axis of $g$ is computed from $g$ alone; the sliding line never enters the formula.

$$g(x)=x^{2}+1$$

$$x=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$x=0$$

The axis stays the vertical line $x=0$ for every $t$. The line $f_0$ is the horizontal axis $y=0$, a different line.

$$
f_0(x)=0,\qquad \text{is }y = 0,\text{ not }x
$$

$$f_0(x)=0$$

A vertical axis $x=0$ and a horizontal line $y=0$ meet at the origin, but they are not the same line.

The axis of $g$ does not depend on $t$ and does not coincide with $f_0$.

solution_overview:
The parabola is fixed and the line slides through the origin as the slope $t$ varies.

$$
g(x) = x^{2}+1,\qquad f_t(x) = tx
$$

Meetings solve $g(x)=tx$, which rearranges to a quadratic in $x$ whose coefficients still depend on $t$.

$$g(x)-f_t(x)=x^{2}-tx+1$$

The discriminant of that family is a quadratic in the parameter, and its sign sorts the geometry into miss, tangency, and two crossings.

$$
\Delta(t) = t^{2}-4 = (t-2)(t+2)
$$

Miss when $|t|<2$ (in particular $t=0$ gives $x^{2}+1=0$, no real $x$), tangency at the two values $t=\pm 2$, and two meetings when $|t|>2$. For $t=3$ one has $\Delta=5>0$, so the graphs meet twice rather than miss.

$$|t|<2:\\ \text{none}\qquad |t|=2:\\ \text{tangent}\qquad |t|>2:\\ \text{two}$$

The axis of $g$ is read from its own coefficients and never sees $t$.

$$
x = 0,\qquad \mathrm{ver} = \left(0,1\right),\qquad a = 1
$$

title: Rebuild from vertex and a point
context: A parabola has vertex $(2,-3)$ and passes through $(0,5)$. It opens upwards. Rebuild its rule and test the claims. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The stretch factor in vertex form equals $2$, so the rebuilt rule is $g(x)=2(x-2)^{2}-3$.
$g(4)=g(0)=5$, matching the symmetry of a parabola about $x=2$.
$g(1)=-1$ and $g(3)=-1$, so those two inputs sit equally far from the axis $x=2$.
The vertex lies above the horizontal axis, and therefore both given points $(0,5)$ and $(2,-3)$ have positive height.
The rule is $g(x)=(x-2)^{2}-3$.

**A.** → True

Vertex form with the given turning point is $g(x)=a(x-2)^{2}-3$. Passing through $(0,5)$ fixes the unknown stretch $a$.

$$g(0)=a(0-2)^{2}-3$$

$$g(0)=5$$

$$4a-3=5$$

$$a=2$$

$$g(x)=2(x-2)^{2}-3$$

Without that stretch the vertex form $(x-2)^{2}-3$ would miss $(0,5)$ by four units, so the leading $2$ is forced.

$$P=4\cdot 2-3$$

$$P=5$$

The rebuilt rule is $2(x-2)^{2}-3$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The points $x=0$ and $x=4$ sit equally far from the axis $x=2$, so a parabola takes the same value at both. The given point $(0,5)$ therefore already names $g(4)$.

$$g(x)=2(x-2)^{2}-3$$

$$g(4)=2(4-2)^{2}-3$$

$$g(4)=5$$

$$g(4)=g(0)$$

Symmetry about $x=2$ is the identity $g(2+t)=g(2-t)$. Here $t=2$ pairs the given intercept with $x=4$.

$$g(2+2)=g(2-2)$$

$$g(2+2)=5$$

Both heights equal $5$, matching the symmetry of a parabola about $x=2$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Vertex form with the given turning point and the given point $(0,5)$ forces stretch $a=2$. Then evaluate at $x=1$ and at the reflected input $x=3$.

$$g(x)=2(x-2)^{2}-3$$

$$g(1)=2(1-2)^{2}-3$$

$$g(1)=-1$$

$$g(1)=g(3)$$

The same identity $g(2+t)=g(2-t)$ with $t=1$ pairs $x=1$ with $x=3$, so the two heights cannot differ.

$$g(2+1)=g(2-1)$$

$$g(2+1)=-1$$

Both heights equal $-1$, matching the equal distance from the axis $x=2$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The vertex is the given turning point $(2,-3)$. Its height is already negative, so it does not lie above the axis, and $(2,-3)$ itself is a given point of negative height.

$$g(2)=-3$$

$$-3<0$$

The other given point $(0,5)$ does have positive height, but that cannot rescue the vertex.

$$(2,-3)\text{ is below }y=0$$

Opening upwards with a negative vertex height is the usual picture of a trough below the axis, not a peak above it.

The vertex lies below the axis, and $(2,-3)$ is not of positive height.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The claimed rule is vertex form with stretch $1$ instead of the $a=2$ that hits $(0,5)$. Check it against that given point.

$$(0-2)^{2}-3=1\neq 5$$

Forgetting the stretch misses the given $y$-intercept. The correct rule, forced by $g(0)=5$, keeps the leading $2$.

$$g(x)=2(x-2)^{2}-3$$

Vertex form always carries a stretch $a\neq 0$; setting $a=1$ by default is the trap that misses the given point.

The unstretched formula is not the rule.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
A vertex and a second point determine a unique parabola of the completed-square shape $a(x-h)^{2}+k$, and the stem already names both $h$ and $k$.

$$g(x)=a(x-2)^{2}-3$$

The extra point $(0,5)$ fixes the stretch $a$. Substitute $x=0$ and solve the one-step equation.

$$a(0-2)^{2}-3=5$$

$$
4a = 8,\qquad a = 2
$$

The rebuilt rule is therefore

$$
g(x) = 2(x-2)^{2}-3 = 2x^{2}-8x+5
$$

The axis is the vertical line through the given vertex, and evaluating at the two symmetric inputs $x=0$ and $x=4$ gives the same height $5$.

$$
\text{axis}:\ x = 2,\qquad g(0) = 5,\qquad g(4) = 5
$$

The vertex height $-3$ lies below the horizontal axis, so the turning point is a trough rather than a peak above $y=0$. Because $a=2>0$ the arms open upwards, matching the stem.

$$
\mathrm{ver} = \left(2,-3\right),\qquad a = 2>0
$$

title: Line inside a square — axis of the other order
context: Let $f(x)=x+1$ and $g(x)=x^{2}$. Study the nested rules $g(f(x))$ and $f(g(x))$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The nested rule $g(f(x))$ expands to a perfect square, so its vertex lies on the horizontal axis.
The nested rule $f(g(x))$ has the same axis of symmetry as $g$.
The two nested rules are identical as functions.
The nested rules $g(f(x))$ and $f(g(x))$ have the same vertex.
The highest power appearing in $f(g(x))$ is $x^{3}$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Nesting the line inside the square substitutes a first-degree expression for $x$, so expand the square.

$$g(f(x))=(x+1)^{2}$$

$$g(f(x))=x^{2}+2x+1$$

A perfect square $(x+1)^{2}$ vanishes at $x=-1$ and is never negative, so the vertex sits on the horizontal axis.

$$g(f(-1))=0$$

A vertex on the axis is the geometric form of a double root at $x=-1$, visible as the square $(x+1)^{2}$.

The nesting is a perfect square whose vertex lies on the axis.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

In this order the square is computed first and the line is applied afterwards, which merely shifts the values vertically.

$$f(g(x))=x^{2}+1$$

A vertical shift leaves the axis of symmetry untouched: both $x^{2}$ and $x^{2}+1$ turn on the vertical coordinate axis.

$$x=-\frac{0}{2\cdot 1}$$

$$x=-\frac{0}{2}$$

$$x=0$$

An operation performed on the values can only stretch or slide the graph vertically, which cannot move a vertical axis.

The composite $f(g(x))$ has the same axis as $g$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The two expansions already differ by the middle term $2x$. A concrete input makes the gap visible.

$$g(f(x))=(x+1)^{2}$$

$$g(f(x))=x^{2}+2x+1$$

$$f(g(x))=x^{2}+1$$

At $x=1$ one composite equals $4$ and the other equals $2$. Equal highest powers do not make the maps identical.

$$g(f(1)) = 4\neq 2$$

$$f(g(x))=f(g(1))$$

Equal highest powers do not make two polynomials the same function: the linear term $2x$ is present in one expansion and absent in the other.

The nested rules are not the same function.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Completing the square isolates the axis shift from half the middle coefficient, then restores the constant so the rewritten formula matches the original polynomial.

$$g(x)=x^{2}$$

Halve the middle coefficient of the monic quadratic factor.

$$\frac{b}{2a}=0$$

$$\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2=0$$

The axis shift is the opposite of that half-coefficient.

$$h=-\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$h=0$$

Evaluate the original rule at the axis to read the completed-square height.

$$g(0)=(0)^{2}+(0)\cdot(0)+(0)$$

$$g(0)=0+(0)+(0)$$

$$g(0)=0$$

Assemble the stretch, the shift, and the height.

$$g(x)=x^{2}$$

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

A line applied after a square can only stretch and shift the values, so the highest power stays $x^{2}$. Nesting multiplies highest powers instead of adding them.

$$f(g(x))=x^{2}+1$$

The product of the degrees is $1\cdot 2=2$, not $1+2=3$. No $x^{3}$ term is produced.

$$\text{highest power }x^{2},\text{ not }x^{3}$$

Take the inner square $g(x)=x^{2}$ of degree $2$ and the outer line of degree $1$: the composite has degree $2$, with no $x^{3}$ term to invent.

The highest power in $f(g(x))$ is $x^{2}$, not $x^{3}$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The stem names a line and a parabola, and the letters ask for both nestings, so expand each composition once and keep the two polynomials.

$$
f(x) = x+1,\qquad g(x) = x^{2}
$$

Feeding the line into the parabola squares the whole linear expression.

$$
g(f(x)) = (x+1)^{2} = x^{2}+2x+1
$$

Feeding the parabola into the line only shifts the square by a constant.

$$f(g(x))=x^{2}+1$$

Both results are quadratic — nesting a line with a parabola cannot raise the highest power above $x^{2}$ — but the coefficients differ, so the two nested rules are different functions. A single test point already separates them.

$$
g(f(1)) = 4,\qquad f(g(1)) = 2
$$

The highest power in $f(g(x))$ is $x^{2}$, not $x^{3}$. Substituting a degree-$1$ rule into a degree-$2$ rule (or the other way around) multiplies those degrees and leaves a quadratic.

$$f(g(x))=x^{2}+1,\qquad \text{highest power }x^{2}\text{ (not }x^{3})$$

title: Scaled product — Vieta with a leading $2$
context: Let $g(x)=2(x-1)(x-5)$. Decide each claim from the factored form. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The sum of the roots equals $6$, and therefore the axis of symmetry is $x=3$.
The vertex height equals $-8$, which is twice the height one would get by dropping the leading $2$.
The values $g(0)$ and $g(6)$ agree, so $x=0$ and $x=6$ sit equally far from the axis.

tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A product $2(x-1)(x-5)$ vanishes precisely where a factor vanishes, so the roots are $1$ and $5$ regardless of the leading $2$.

$$x=1$$

$$
x=5,\qquad 1+5 = 6
$$

The axis is the midpoint of those two roots, which is also $x=-b/(2a)$ after expanding.

$$x=\frac{1+5}{2}$$

$$x=\frac{6}{2}$$

$$x=3$$

A leading coefficient stretches the graph vertically and does not move the zeros, so the axis is still the midpoint of $1$ and $5$.

The sum of the roots is $6$ and the axis is $x=3$.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The vertex sits on the axis $x=3$, the midpoint of the roots $1$ and $5$. Evaluate the factored form there, keeping the leading $2$.

$$g(3)=2(3-1)(3-5)$$

$$g(3)=2\cdot 2\cdot(-2)$$

$$g(3)=-8$$

Dropping the leading $2$ would have produced $-4$, half of the true height. The stretch doubles that dropped-leading trap.

$$g(3)=-4\neq -8$$

The vertex height is $-8$, twice the height one would get by dropping the leading $2$.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The axis bisects the roots $1$ and $5$, so it is $x=3$. The inputs $0$ and $6$ sit three units on either side, hence a parabola takes the same value at both.

$$g(0)=2(-1)(-5)$$

$$g(0)=10$$

$$g(6)=2(5)(1)$$

$$g(6)=10$$

Symmetry about $x=3$ is $g(3+t)=g(3-t)$. The pair $t=3$ recovers $x=0$ and $x=6$ with a common height $10$.

$$g(3+3)=g(3-3)$$

$$g(3+3)=10$$

Those two heights agree, so $x=0$ and $x=6$ sit equally far from the axis.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → True

The constant term is the value at the origin, which the factored form gives without a full expansion.

$$g(0)=2(-1)(-5)$$

$$g(0)=10$$

Vieta's product is that constant over the leading coefficient, which is also the product of the named roots.

$$P=\frac{10}{2}$$

$$P=5$$

$$P=1\cdot 5$$

The product of the roots is independent of the leading $2$ once it is cancelled in $c/a$, which is why $P=5$ matches $1\cdot 5$.

Constant term $10$ and product of roots $5$ both match.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Expand the inner product first, then distribute the leading $2$. The middle coefficient comes from the sum of the roots, scaled by $-2$.

$$(x-1)(x-5)=x^{2}-6x+5$$

$$2(x^{2}-6x+5)=2x^{2}-12x+10$$

The trap $-10$ is what one would get from $2\times(-5)$ if the inner sum of roots had been taken to be $5$ instead of $6$.

$$2(x^{2}-6x+5)=-12\neq -10$$

The middle coefficient of $a(x-r)(x-s)$ is

$$-a(r+s)=-2\cdot 6$$

$$-a(r+s)=-12$$

not $-2\cdot 5$.

The middle coefficient is $-12$, not $-10$.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
The parabola is already factored, so the roots can be read off the brackets before any expansion.

$$g(x)=2(x-1)(x-4)$$

The zeros are $x=1$ and $x=4$. Their midpoint is the axis, and Vieta will confirm the same midpoint after expanding.

$$
x = 1,\qquad x = 4,\qquad x = \frac{5}{2}
$$

Expanding once produces the three coefficients every later letter needs.

$$g(x)=2x^{2}-10x+8$$

The middle coefficient is $-10$ and the constant term is $8$. The vertex height is the value of $g$ on the axis, not the constant term and not $-4$.

$$
g\left(\frac{5}{2}\right) = 2\cdot\frac{25}{4}-10\cdot\frac{5}{2}+8 = -\frac{9}{2}
$$

$$
S = 5,\qquad P = 4,\qquad \Delta_{g} = 36,\qquad \mathrm{ver} = \left(\frac{5}{2},-\frac{9}{2}\right)
$$

Because the leading coefficient $2$ is positive the arms open upwards and this vertex is a trough.

title: Parabola figure, line table — a combined reading
context: The figure shows an unknown parabola $g$ (solid brown; no formula). Separately, the table lists an unknown line $\ell$ at four inputs. Use the figure for claims about $g$ and the table for claims about $\ell$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

An even upward parabola $x^{2}-4$ turns at the origin, so the trough height is the constant term, already $-4$ on the vertical scale.

Checking the remaining columns recovers the listed heights: $2\cdot 1+1=3$, $2\cdot 2+1=5$, $2\cdot 3+1=7$.

$$\ell(3)=7$$

title: Dock crane — stretch from a named vertex
context: A dock crane's clearance is modelled by a parabola $g$ that opens downwards, turns at $(1,6)$, and meets the deck $y=0$ at $x=-1$ and $x=3$. A linear sensor path $f$ passes through $(0,2)$ with slope $-1$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The rule for $g$ is $g(x)=-(x+1)(x-3)$, and this unscaled product already peaks at height $6$.
The unscaled product $-(x+1)(x-3)$ already equals $6$ at $x=1$, so the stretch needed to hit the named vertex is $k=-1$.
The sensor path is $f(x)=-x+3$, because a slope $-1$ through $(0,2)$ lifts the intercept to $3$.
The sensor path and the clearance curve meet at exactly one real point.
At $x=1$ the sensor lies strictly below the clearance peak.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Opening downwards with those roots means $g(x)=k(x+1)(x-3)$ for some $k<0$. The unscaled choice $k=-1$ still has to hit height $6$ at the named peak $x=1$.

$$-(1+1)(1-3)=-(2)(-2)$$

$$h=-(1+1)(1-3)$$

$$h=4$$

$$4\neq 6$$

The unscaled factorisation misses the named vertex height. A stretch other than $-1$ is required.

The stretch $k$ is fixed by the named vertex: $k(1+1)(1-3)=6$ forces $k=-3/2$, not the unscaled $-1$.

$$k=-\frac{3}{2}$$

The unscaled product does not already peak at height $6$.

So the statement is False.

**B.** → False

Evaluate the unscaled product at the named peak abscissa $x=1$; that value is its vertex height, and it is the stretch that would have to equal $6$.

$$
-(x+1)(x-3)\big|_{x = 1} = -(2)(-2) = 4
$$

$$4\neq 6$$

The unscaled vertex height is $4$, not $6$, so the stretch needed to hit the named vertex is not $k=-1$. Matching $k\cdot(-4)=6$ would force $k=-3/2$.

The unscaled product is $4$ at $x=1$, not $6$.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

A line is uniquely determined by its slope and a point. Slope $-1$ through $(0,2)$ is point-slope with intercept $2$, not $3$.

$$f(x)=-1\cdot(x-0)+2$$

$$f(x)=-x+2$$

The claimed intercept $3$ would have required the line to pass through $(0,3)$ instead of the given $(0,2)$.

$$f(x)=-x+2\neq -x+3$$

Point-slope through $(0,2)$ never lifts the intercept. The claimed $+3$ would be the intercept of a parallel line through $(0,3)$.

The intercept is $2$, not $3$.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Scale so that $g(1)=6$: $k(2)(-2)=6$ forces $k=-3/2$. Then form the difference with the sensor $f(x)=-x+2$.

$$g(x)=-\frac{3}{2}(x+1)(x-3)$$

$$g(x)-f(x)=-\frac{3}{2}x^{2}+4x+\frac{5}{2}$$

$$\Delta=16+15$$

$$\Delta=31$$

$$31>0$$

A positive discriminant gives two distinct real meetings, not one. Tangency would have required $\Delta=0$.

A quadratic difference with positive discriminant cannot be a perfect square, so tangency is out of reach for this pair.

The graphs meet twice, not once.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

At the peak abscissa compare the sensor height with the named vertex height $6$. Only the line is needed: the sensor is $f(x)=-x+2$.

$$f(1)=-1+2$$

$$f(1)=1$$

$$1<6$$

The sensor sits five units below the clearance peak. A meeting at $x=1$ would have required $f(1)=6$, which fails.

The clearance peak is the given point $(1,6)$, while the sensor at that abscissa is the much lower point $(1,1)$.

$$(1,1)\text{ sits below }(1,6)$$

The sensor lies strictly below the clearance peak.

So the statement is True.
solution_overview:
The clearance brief names a downward parabola by its vertex and its two deck meetings, together with a sensor line through $(0,2)$ of slope $-1$. Those data determine both rules uniquely.

$$g(x)=a(x+1)(x-3)$$

The unscaled product $-(x+1)(x-3)$ already has the right roots and the right axis, but its height at $x=1$ is $4$, not $5$. The stretch $a$ must make up the missing unit.

$$-(1+1)(1-3)=4\neq 5$$

$$
a(2)(-2) = 5,\qquad a = -\frac{5}{4}
$$

The rebuilt clearance curve and the sensor path are therefore

$$
g(x) = -\frac{5}{4}(x+1)(x-3),\qquad f(x) = -x+2
$$

The claimed sensor $f(x)=-x+3$ would pass through $(0,3)$, not through the given point $(0,2)$. Meetings of $g$ with the true sensor are the zeros of $g-f$; that discriminant is positive, so there are two real meetings rather than one.

$$
g(x)-f(x) = -\frac{5}{4}x^{2}+\frac{7}{2}x+\frac{7}{4},\qquad \Delta = 21
$$

At the crown abscissa $x=1$ the sensor sits at height $1$, strictly below the clearance peak $5$.

$$
g(1) = 5,\qquad f(1) = 1
$$

title: Two nestings — missing linear term, shifted axis
context: Let $f(x)=2x-1$ and $g(x)=x^{2}-4$. Compare $f(g(x))$ with $g(f(x))$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The nested rule $f(g(x))$ equals $2x^{2}-9$, which has no linear term, and its vertex is $(0,-9)$.
The nested rule $g(f(x))$ equals $4x^{2}-4x-3$, whose axis is $x=\frac{1}{2}$ and whose vertex height is $-4$.

tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

In this order the parabola is computed first and the line is applied afterwards, which merely rescales and shifts the values.

No $x$ term remains, so the axis is $x=0$ and the vertex height is the constant term $-9$.

$$f(g(0))=-9\qquad\text{vertex }(0,-9)$$

Because only even powers survive, the composite is even about the $y$-axis, which is the geometric meaning of a missing linear term.

$$f(g(-x))=2x^{2}-9$$

$$f(g(-x))=f(g(x))$$

The nesting is $2x^{2}-9$ with vertex $(0,-9)$.

**B.** → True

The axis is

$$x=-\\frac{b}{2a}$$

$$x=4/(8)$$

$$x=1/2$$

and the vertex height is the value of the composite there.

$$g\bigl(f(\tfrac{1}{2})\bigr)=0-4$$

$$g\bigl(f(\tfrac{1}{2})\bigr)=-4$$

The axis formula on $4x^{2}-4x-3$ uses only the first two coefficients and ignores the constant $-3$.

$$x=-\frac{-4}{2\cdot 4}$$

$$x=-\frac{-4}{8}$$

$$x=\frac{1}{2}$$

Axis $x=\frac{1}{2}$ and vertex height $-4$ both match.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Nesting a degree-$1$ rule with a degree-$2$ rule multiplies those degrees instead of adding them, so both composites have highest power $x^{2}$.

$$1\cdot 2=2$$

$$f(g(x))=2x^{2}-9$$

$$g(f(x))=4x^{2}-4x-3$$

A cubic would have required nesting a degree-$2$ rule inside another degree-$2$ rule. A line and a parabola cannot produce $x^{3}$.

Each leading coefficient is non-zero, so neither composite drops degree. Both nested rules have the same highest power $x^{2}$.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

$$f(g(x))=2x^{2}-9$$

$$f(g(-x))=2x^{2}-9$$

$$f(g(-x))=f(g(x))$$

The other order $g(f(x))=4x^{2}-4x-3$ does have a linear term, which is why the two nestings are not interchangeable.

There is no linear term, and the graph is symmetric about the vertical axis.

**E.** → False

$$f(g(0))=f(-4)$$

$$f(g(0))=-9$$

$$g(f(0))=g(-1)$$

$$g(f(0))=-3$$

$$g(f(0))=-9\neq -3$$

Composition does not commute: substituting the parabola into the line is a vertical stretch of $x^{2}-4$, while the other order shifts the input first.

solution_overview:
The stem names a line and a shifted parabola, and the letters compare both nestings, so expand each composition once.

$$
f(x) = 2x-1,\qquad g(x) = x^{2}-4
$$

Feeding the parabola into the line scales and then shifts the square; no linear term survives.

$$

Feeding the line into the parabola squares the whole linear expression and then subtracts $4$.

$$

$$

title: Opposite roots — evenness and the trough sign
context: Let $g(x)=(x+3)(x-3)$. Decide each claim. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The axis is the midpoint $x=0$ of the bracket zeros, the vertex is $(0,-9)$, and therefore $g$ is even: $g(-x)=g(x)$.

**A.** → True

$$g(0)=(3)(-3)$$

$$g(0)=-9\qquad\text{vertex }(0,-9)$$

Expanding displays only even powers, which is evenness: $g(-x)=g(x)$ for every $x$.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-9$$

$$g(x)=g(-x)$$

Evenness is the identity $g(-x)=g(x)$, which for a quadratic holds if and only if the middle coefficient vanishes, as it does here.

$$b=0$$

Axis $x=0$, vertex $(0,-9)$, and $g$ is even.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

An odd function would satisfy $g(-x)=-g(x)$ and in particular $g(0)=0$. Here $g(0)=-9\neq 0$ already kills oddness. A concrete test point confirms the sides differ.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-9$$

$$
g(-2)=-5,\qquad -g(2) = 5
$$

$g$ is even, not odd. A product of opposite linear factors is a difference of squares, which is even.

$$g(-2)=-5\neq 5$$

The only function that is both even and odd is $0$. A difference of squares with a nonzero constant term cannot be odd.

$$g(0)=-9\neq 0$$

$g$ is even, not odd.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → False

The brackets name the roots directly as $x=-3$ and $x=3$. One of those is negative, so they are not both positive.

$$g(x)=(x+3)(x-3)$$

$$x=-3$$

$$x=3$$

The axis is their midpoint $x=0$, which is the origin itself, not a line to the right of the origin.

Opposite roots $\pm 3$ place the axis at the origin, which is neither to the right nor to the left.

$$x=\frac{-3+3}{2}$$

$$x=\frac{0}{2}$$

$$x=0$$

The roots are not both positive, and the axis is not to the right of the origin.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The vertex height is $g(0)=-9$, not $+9$. The sign trap is the constant term of $x^{2}-9$: flipping that sign would turn a trough into a peak of the wrong function.

$$g(0)=(3)(-3)$$

$$g(0)=-9$$

$$g(0)=(0,-9)\neq(0,9)$$

An upward parabola with a negative constant term turns below the axis, not above it.

Flipping the sign of the constant term would produce $x^{2}+9$, a different parabola whose trough sits at $(0,9)$ above the axis.

$$g(0)=x^{2}+9\neq x^{2}-9$$

The vertex is $(0,-9)$, not $(0,9)$.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → False

An upward parabola with vertex height $-9$ takes negative values between its roots. It is also not a square of a single linear factor: $(x-3)^{2}$ would vanish only at $x=3$.

$$g(x)=x^{2}-9$$

$$g(0)=-9$$

$$-9<0$$

Between $x=-3$ and $x=3$ the graph sits below the axis, so $g$ is not everywhere non-negative.

$$g(x)\ge 0\text{ fails on }(-3,3)$$

A square of a single linear factor would be $(x-3)^{2}$ or $(x+3)^{2}$, each with a double root, not two simple opposite roots.

$g$ is not everywhere non-negative.

So the statement is False.
solution_overview:
Opposite roots $x=\pm 3$ make the axis the vertical coordinate axis and make $g$ an even function. Expand once to see the missing linear term.

$$
g(x) = (x+3)(x-3) = x^{2}-9
$$

There is no $x$ term, so $g(-x)=g(x)$ for every $x$: the graph is symmetric about the $y$-axis, which is therefore the axis of symmetry. An odd rule would have required $g(-x)=-g(x)$, which fails as soon as $g$ is even and not identically zero.

$$
g(-x) = (-x)^{2}-9 = g(x)\neq -g(x)
$$

The vertex sits on that axis at height $-9$, the lowest point of an upward parabola, not at $(0,9)$.

$$
\mathrm{ver} = \left(0,-9\right),\qquad a = 1>0
$$

The two roots are $3$ and $-3$, so they are not both positive. Between them $g$ is negative, so the inequality $g(x)\ge 0$ fails on $(-3,3)$.

$$
S = 0,\qquad P = -9,\qquad \Delta_{g} = 36
$$

$$g(0)=-9<0$$

title: Revenue peak is not the profit peak

$$a=1$$

Then

matching the last listed height.

solution_overview:
